canonSays.says: A plan is a distinct object holding candidate steps; each step has dependencies, deadlines, outcome-keyed branches, resources and a disposition (chosen, declined with reason, done, blocked); a declined step 'keeps its reason and stays visible'.

Every element carries a support status (established, short of the standard, hypothetical), displayed wherever it is 'in the same treatment everywhere, exactly as undetermined is'; a hypothetical premise is hunch debt.
The machine may suggest a plan as candidates and check it (e.g. an outcome with no next step); it never adopts a step.
The plan is working material and never published; if that changes it applies only to plans written afterwards.

openQuestions.whyOpen: No requirement or module holds a plan, so none is built. Undecided: how to draw an outcome-keyed decision tree legibly, how support status shows on every element, how a plan relates to the escalation module's built seven-stage protocol (which also sequences outward acts), and how refusing an outward act whose step is not 'established' appears.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: Nothing for plans; individual action pages exist (risk tier, governing laws, correspondence).
related: Q25 (declared flows; plans must not share their machinery)
Q6 (support status reuses the undetermined treatment)

options.option: A tree/graph view with each step as a card (support status, deadline, resources list, disposition), branches labelled by outcome, declined steps greyed but present
options.tradeoffs: Matches Bob's 'dependency graphs keyed to outcomes'; graphs are hard on phones and in print.

options.option: An outline (nested list) of steps with 'if denied / if ignored' sub-steps, and a separate declined-options list
options.tradeoffs: Readable anywhere and simple to build; branching is less visible.

options.option: Fold the plan into escalation stages rather than a separate object
options.tradeoffs: Reuses built code; conflicts with Case Making §2, since an escalation is one pursued breach, not a set of options.

openQuestions.recommendation: The second option first (an outline with support status on every line), with a graph view added later; a module requirement must be written before design goes deep.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob: a plan needs requirements and a module (scope and tranche are his); Design settles the layout once he does.

elsewhere.note: Bob moved this question to a separate session on Actions, which decides it (DEC-93); BOB's action-plan rulings 1-10 there rule it in part.
elsewhere.src: DECISIONS.md DEC-93; docs/development/action-design/ACTION-PLAN.md (another session's branch, as BOB's page cites it)

rulings: D1-D6 and the closing rule of 2026-09-30 (K590)
ruled.decided: The plan page is an outline, not a graph: its subjects with their support; its options collapsed to a one-line summary, category and dates, sortable by category, date, subject or disposition, with declined options kept visible with their reasons; up to three scenarios of phases with checkpoints and branches that a member judges; and what each started option became. A strip under the title shows the checks in words. The assistant's suggestions wait in a separate tray until adopted. It holds no costs, budgets, assignees or scores and is never published. A graph view may come later. Layout detail remains Design's. The approved sketch is views/plan-page.html.
ruled.title: The action plan page

openQuestions.question: What does the assistant dialog look like on each surface, and how is 'the machine did the looking, you do the concluding' made felt?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: The assistant is one way in everywhere and must never appear to conclude; the pilot flow and wizard are unbuilt.
openQuestions.context: The assistant is a text or voice box available on every screen. A member can ask it to find something, help with a task, create something, or take an act. It may search, gather and check, but it never concludes, authors a reason or signs; for multi-step work it acts as a guide that opens the right screen and waits while the member acts.

canonSays.says: 'The machine may do the looking; the member does the concluding.'

One way in on every surface, a persistent tag expanding to a dialog (S12); the assistant may initiate an act but the act 'still runs its four beats'; it is a named non-member actor ('the assistant did this, at Anna's request').
It shows how it read the request; asks at most one clarifying question; an answer names the level searched ('I found nothing' without a level is the overclaim).
The wizard is a plan rendered as steps, 'visibly machine-made, dismissible, never blocking'; it 'never enters values into fields and never presses Submit'; an abandoned wizard is a non-event.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The rules are clear but the pilot flow and wizard are unbuilt, and nothing says how the dialog looks, where it sits on each surface, or what signals machine output versus member text. Only CHECK runs are deployed, so the dialog must explain refused modes. Showing voice transcription for correction is undesigned.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: No prompt box anywhere; only a running-session indicator for AI runs.

options.option: A side panel docked beside the owning surface; machine text in a distinct 'machine work' style with attribution; each wizard step highlights the real control but never fills it
options.tradeoffs: The member always acts on the real surface; needs space and a consistent machine style across the product.

options.option: A modal dialog that navigates away and returns
options.tradeoffs: Simple on phones; hides the surface the member is meant to act on, weakening 'you do the concluding'.

openQuestions.recommendation: The first option: a docked panel with one visible 'machine work' treatment shared with every other machine output, and acts always performed on the real surface.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Design, within DEC-24, DEC-27 and ASSISTANT-PILOT; Bob only if the pilot's read-only scope or its order is to change.

ruled.decided: the assistant is a panel docked beside the surface it serves, and it never floats. Its text carries the one 'machine work' treatment every machine output shares, with attribution ('the assistant did this, at <member>'s request'); a wizard step highlights the real control and never fills or presses it, and the member performs every act on the real surface. Two refinements: the panel expands (a draggable divider and an 'expand' control let it take most of the window while some of the member's surface stays visible; it shrinks back by itself when a wizard step needs the member to act; its size is remembered, and one click restores the default), and it docks by screen shape, at the side on wide screens and at the bottom on narrow ones, with the member free to switch edges and the choice remembered.
ruled.title: The assistant panel

openQuestions.question: What does a newcomer learn first, and how do starter materials and onboarding fit a first session?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Design Requirement 11 requires usability within one session by someone with no civic experience; starter materials are not started.
openQuestions.context: A newcomer is someone just invited to a group: they open the invitation link, choose a handle (the name the record shows) and a password, and land in the product. Before they can usefully capture, weigh or publish, they need the group's values, how evidence is graded, and how to stay safe. The canon calls the learning materials the 'starter kit'.

canonSays.says: The starter kit (values and principles explained, a walkthrough of a real case, data-source and legal-tool guides, a security guide) must be 'usable within one session' by someone with no civic experience, free at believeinoakland.org.
'All starter kit materials', the explanatory paragraphs and the security guide are 'not yet started'.
Load-bearing state is 'named explicitly so a newcomer can recognize it and learn its implications'.
Informing at the act, once, is respect; 'responsibility reminders detached from any act' are the flaw.
The product must not carry Oakland-specific references that tell a group elsewhere it is not for them.

openQuestions.whyOpen: No module covers UC-148: nothing says what the first session contains, in what order, or whether the kit lives in the product or on a website. Two tensions: Requirement 11 names Oakland sources, tools and case, while the 2026-09-25 ruling bars local content from the product; and DEC-69 forbids act-detached 'responsibility' lessons, so a front-loaded tutorial risks being the nagging the canon calls a flaw.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: No onboarding or starter kit; newcomers get hover glossary definitions and short 'teach' paragraphs on each surface, and the invitation page shows cover, role and capabilities.

options.option: Teach at the act only: no tutorial; every first encounter with an act or state carries its one-time explanation, plus a public starter kit on the group's website outside the product.
options.tradeoffs: Fully consistent with DEC-69 and cheap; a newcomer never gets the big picture (values, security) unless they find the website.

options.option: A short in-product 'first session' path: values and principles, a security briefing, then a guided walkthrough of one real published case read end to end, with jurisdiction-specific guides supplied by the group's installed profile.
options.tradeoffs: Meets Requirement 11 inside the product and keeps local content in profiles; costs authoring a generic sample case and per-profile guides.

options.option: A practice sandbox: the newcomer captures, grades and drafts in a scratch space with a sample case, then enters the real record.
options.tradeoffs: Most effective learning; a second, practice world risks confusion with the real record.

openQuestions.recommendation: Option 2, with option 1's teach-at-the-act rule everywhere else: it satisfies Requirement 11 in one session while keeping local guides in jurisdiction profiles, not in the product.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob: what a newcomer must learn first, and whether the starter kit is part of the product or the group's website, is a requirement and UX principle; the layout of the path is Design's.

ruled.decided: Deferred: 'this needs to be deferred until the new UX is in place and stabilized.' Onboarding is designed against the product members will actually use. Meanwhile the measures map already rules that a newcomer meets strength against the bar and 'Undetermined' first, everything else taught at the act (DEC-82).
ruled.trigger: The redesigned member surfaces are built and have been stable in use (no major layout changes) for a period BOB judges sufficient; or Bob asks.
ruled.title: What a newcomer learns first

openQuestions.question: How are the five trust levels (our work, independently verified, meets standards, not yet evaluated, flagged) shown on information from other groups?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Trust signals must be ambient and travel with data; no requirement holds the indicator.
openQuestions.context: Members often use work that someone else produced, above all another group's published case. The Roadmap wants every piece of information to carry a visible trust indicator with five levels, from 'our own work' down to 'flagged concerns', so a member can tell at a glance how far to lean on it. A member meets it when reading or citing material they did not produce.

canonSays.says: 'Every piece of information carries a visible trust indicator': our work; independently verified; meets standards (compliance skill); not yet evaluated; flagged concerns. Signals are 'ambient (always visible)' (§12).

canonSays.source: Functional Architecture v3 'Trust signals throughout the stack'
canonSays.says: The signal travels with the data; 'independently verified' comes from the group re-evaluating incoming work before citing it.
Bob revised 'no transitive trust': inherited trust is accepted if disclosed; what is inherited is 'the fact of publication, never the credibility of the content'.
A leg citing a published case is 'inherited', names an edition, and cannot be stronger than that edition's frozen strength.
The five-level indicator and a group's acceptance into its own body of work are covered by no requirement.

openQuestions.whyOpen: No module produces the levels: nothing records that a group verified or accepted another group's work, and no evaluator of incoming work yields 'meets standards' or 'flagged'. The canon also shifted: the Functional Architecture says incoming work is re-evaluated before citation, while Bob's 2026-07-30 ruling and inquiry R7 let a member cite a published edition directly. Whether the levels replace, sit beside or derive from the record's own grades is undecided.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: Nothing: no trust dots; a published case shows its frozen strength per finding and a stranger can verify its signature.

options.option: Derive the levels from facts the record already holds: ours (produced here); inherited (another group's published edition, signature verified); accepted (a recorded acceptance act, new); not yet evaluated; flagged only when a recorded evaluation names issues.
options.tradeoffs: Honest and ambient with little new doctrine; needs one new act (accept into our body of work) and drops or defers 'meets standards' until an evaluator exists.

options.option: Build the Roadmap's five levels as written, including a compliance evaluation of incoming work.
options.tradeoffs: Faithful to the Roadmap; requires a new evaluation module and risks a machine verdict reading as a trust grade, which the 'machine proposes, member decides' rule resists.

options.option: Drop a separate trust indicator and rely on grades, provenance chain and edition shown everywhere.
options.tradeoffs: No new construct; loses the at-a-glance signal the Roadmap requires and the idea of a group's accepted body of work.

openQuestions.recommendation: Option 1: it keeps the ambient signal while grounding every level in a recorded fact, and leaves 'meets standards' for when an evaluator exists.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob: the trust hierarchy is mission doctrine (Roadmap §11) and choosing to revise it, and adding an acceptance act, are requirements; the dot's look is Design's.

ruled.decided: The five levels become an origin mark in the same family as 'Machine work', answering who made this: Ours; Another group's (a published edition, signature verified); Accepted by our group (a new reasoned act, attributed, with a reason); 'Not yet evaluated'; 'Flagged' only when a member's recorded evaluation names specific issues, never a machine's. 'Meets standards' is deferred until an evaluator of incoming work exists. The mark is ambient; a hover shows the fact behind it. It is never composed with grades or strength into one trust score.
stillOpen: What accepting another group's work commits the group to, and whether it can be withdrawn
How a flag is raised, answered and cleared
Whether 'meets standards' returns, and what evaluates it
How the mark travels when a group republishes work it accepted
ruled.title: Where information from other groups came from (the origin mark)

brief.settledBy: DEC-92 (Bob, 2026-09-29) settled the display: the five trust levels become an origin mark ('Ours', 'Another group's', 'Accepted by our group', 'Not yet evaluated', 'Flagged'), ambient, hover shows the fact, never composed into a trust score; folded into Roadmap §11. DEC-92 itself lists what Bob left 'to decide later': 'what accepting another group's work commits the group to and whether it can be withdrawn; how a flag is raised, answered and cleared; whether "meets standards" returns and what evaluates it; how the mark travels when a group republishes work it accepted.' No later K-ruling or requirement touches these four; the acceptance act's requirements are still owed (DEC-92 'owed').
brief.title: Accepting and flagging another group's work
brief.decision: The four points DEC-92 left for later: what 'Accepted by our group' commits the group to and how it is withdrawn; how a 'Flagged' mark is raised, answered and cleared; whether 'meets standards' ever returns; and what the mark says when your group republishes work it accepted.
brief.whyYours: Acceptance is a new act by which a group takes on another group's work, which touches the inherited-trust doctrine ('the fact of publication, never the credibility of the content'). What a group vouches for, and what a flag says about another group, is doctrine; the mark's look is already set by DEC-92.
brief.context:
A 'member' is a person in a group using CivicOS; a 'case' is a group's signed, published argument, released in numbered editions. When members cite another group's case, it now carries an origin mark saying who made it. Two labels need new acts: 'Accepted by our group' and 'Flagged'.

Example: the Alameda Budget Watch has published a case (edition 2) on the sewer fund your group is investigating. A member cites it; it shows 'Another group's · signature verified'. Two members re-check its three key documents, and one clicks 'Accept into our work' and writes why; the mark becomes 'Accepted by our group'. Later another member finds a misread figure and flags it. What did the acceptance promise, does the flag undo it, and what does a reader of your own next case see?

Bob's 2026-07-30 ruling holds that citing never carries over another group's credibility. Acceptance is the one place a group could take that credibility on.
alreadySettled: The mark and its five labels, ambient, hover shows who produced it, which edition, who accepted it and why; never a trust score (DEC-92; Roadmap §11)
'Flagged' only from a member's recorded evaluation naming specific issues, never a machine's (DEC-92)
A cited edition can never be stronger than that edition's frozen strength (inquiry R7; Publication §3 rule 5)
Reasoned acts are corrected only forward; the correction is a further dated act and both stay in the record (DEC-88; Interaction Constructs §A, DEC-19)
Nothing reaches another group except by what it publishes; no outside channel (DEC-94 item 3; Publication pull model)

options.label: A
options.name: Light acceptance, member-owned flags
options.whatTheMemberSees: 'Accept into our work' asks what was checked. The mark becomes 'Accepted by our group'; hover shows who, when and why. Grades and strength do not change. 'Withdraw acceptance' is a reasoned act, and findings resting on the work get a re-evaluation notice. A flag names specific issues and stays inside your group unless you disclose it in your own case; when the other group publishes a new edition, a member clears or keeps the flag with a reason. Republished work reads 'Another group's (Budget Watch, ed. 2), accepted by our group'. 'Meets standards' stays deferred.
options.gains: Every label rests on a recorded act with a name and a reason. It fits the inherited-trust boundary, and a correction is never silent.
options.costs: An acceptance adds no strength, so members may wonder what it is for. It is a statement of the group's stance, not a grade.

options.label: B
options.name: Acceptance as full vouching
options.whatTheMemberSees: Accepting treats the work as the group's own. Its findings can be graded by your members as if you produced them, and the mark reads close to 'Ours'.
options.gains: Matches the Roadmap's 'independently verified (high)'. Accepted work becomes fully usable.
options.costs: Crosses the rule that citing never carries over credibility; honest only with a real re-check process; a careless acceptance could launder another group's errors into your cases.

options.label: C
options.name: Defer until a second group exists
options.whatTheMemberSees: For now only 'Ours', 'Another group's' and 'Not yet evaluated' appear. There is no accept or flag button.
options.gains: Nothing is designed for a situation no group has yet.
options.costs: The requirements DEC-92 owes wait, UC-083 stays uncovered, and members who distrust a cited case have no recorded way to say so.

brief.recommendation: Option A: the smallest set of acts that makes every label an attributed fact, reusing rules Bob already set (correction forward, re-evaluation notices, no outside channel). If 'meets standards' ever returns, it should read as 'Machine work', not as a trust level (my judgement, following DEC-24 and DEC-92).
howToAnswer: As recommended.
As recommended, but a flag is visible to the other group through our published case only when we choose to disclose it.
Option C: wait until a second group is using CivicOS.
Question first: who in our group may accept, any member or only an administrator?
brief.ifLeftOpen: The origin mark ships with 'Ours', 'Another group's' and 'Not yet evaluated' only, and the acceptance act's requirements (inquiry, publication, affordances; owed by DEC-92) cannot be drafted. Nothing else waits.
sources: Declared Bias 'Differential traversal and the cross-group rerun'

openQuestions.question: How is a member told a capture's grade, and whether it is co-attested, at the moment of capture (DEC-51, DEC-81)? Presentation only.
openQuestions.whyItMatters: The belief about what a capture is worth forms at capture; the note is currently discarded before the member sees it.
openQuestions.context: When a member captures a document from a web address, the record fetches it, fingerprints the bytes and gives the capture a grade: how strong it is as evidence of what that address served and when (a direct fetch earns at most B; A needs a chain-of-custody archive). 'Co-attestation' is a separate act that asks an independent timestamp service to record when those bytes existed. The question is what the member is told about the grade at the moment they capture. Since DEC-81, co-attestation also decides what a published case says about the document: a co-attested Grade B can be published as it is, and one whose co-attestation failed only by the owner's acknowledgement, marked 'self-attested only'.

canonSays.says: 'RENDER IT, WHOLE, AT THE MOMENT OF CAPTURE': the plane's grade note is shown when the capture completes, including the co-attestation clause, never split.

The fence wording is the record's and must state the question co-attestation answers: 'when did these bytes exist?'; not whether the document is true; it strengthens a Grade B capture toward evidentiary weight and 'never reaches Grade A'.
The grade note at capture is named as the model of 'informing at the act, once'.
A capture earns a grade (at most B for a direct fetch); an attestation is recorded and never reaches A.

A co-attested Grade B (a trusted timestamp over the digest and a third-party co-archive of the locator) is sufficient to publish; the case discloses each document's grade and whether it is co-attested; a failed co-attestation is retried at the pre-flight, then acknowledged and marked 'self-attested only'; Grade A is the ceiling for adversarial or legal use and is deferred.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The substance is already settled: DEC-51 overturned the discard this question describes, and DEC-39 states what co-attestation is worth, so the question's premise is out of date. What remains open is presentation only: where and how long the note sits after capture, how a bulk or machine-requested capture (which completes later, unattended) carries it, and how the grade looks when the member returns to the document. One real tension: the pre-capture explanation deliberately predicts no grade (the capture does not exist yet), so the member sees nothing about strength until the capture lands.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The Add surface renders the plane's full grade note, co-attestation clause included, right after a capture completes (UI-54), and states no grade beforehand.

options.option: Carry the old interface's treatment forward: the whole note shown once at completion, then the grade chip on the document page from then on.
options.tradeoffs: Already ruled and built; nothing is decided anew. A member capturing many documents sees the same long note repeatedly.

options.option: Show the whole note in full on a member's first capture, and afterwards a one-line grade statement that expands to the whole note.
options.tradeoffs: Less repetition, consistent with 'once'; but DEC-51 said 'whole', so a collapsed default needs Bob to confirm that collapsed-but-present still counts as whole.

options.option: For captures that complete later (bulk or machine-requested), attach the note to the completed-capture status on the document and in the queue's condition item.
options.tradeoffs: Fills the unattended gap; adds nothing new to the record.

options.option: Show at capture whether co-attestation succeeded, since it now decides whether the document can be published without an acknowledgement (DEC-81).
options.tradeoffs: Makes the consequence visible early; adds one more fact to a note DEC-51 requires to stay whole.

openQuestions.recommendation: Option 1 plus option 3 for unattended captures; ask Bob only if Design wants option 2's collapsed form.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Design: DEC-51, DEC-39 and DEC-81 settle the substance; only presentation remains. Bob only if the note is to be shortened or collapsed.

ruled.decided: The whole grade note is shown once, when a capture completes; a capture that completes later and unattended carries the note on the completed capture and on its queue item. The system may suggest that a capture not yet released bears on a member's work, under six guards: it appears where the member already works, never as a notification; it is labelled machine work with its reason; a dismissal is remembered; it never appears during a heavy act; a member may switch it off; and its acceptance rate is measured.
ruled.title: Telling a member a capture's grade
ruled.stillOpen: the held-captures list with bulk triage

brief.settledBy: Only DEC-95 item 2 is open. Bob, correcting DEC-95: 'the held-captures list with bulk triage was proposed but not approved; it stays open.' Items 1 (grade note) and 3 (relevance suggestions) are ruled. Related substance is settled elsewhere: Intake Doctrine §4 allows batch release under conditions ('crucial-criticality or contested material is NEVER batch-released'), and K583 gives the bulk release act to the ratification module (N400, now carried to T19 per T18's current.md).
brief.title: A list of captures nobody has dealt with yet
brief.decision: Should members get a list of their held captures (per member and per project), showing each one's age and letting them sort it and deal with several at once, or should held captures only appear where they bear on work?
brief.whyYours: Bob raised this himself when he extended question 13. It is a UX choice with a doctrine edge: bulk handling makes the batch-release rule and the no-nagging rule (DEC-69, DEC-94) felt in daily work. The list's layout would be Design's.
brief.context:
A 'capture' is a document the record fetched from a web address (or received) and fingerprinted. It lands 'held' (the record's state 'collected'): stored and fully traced, but not yet 'released', meaning vouched for by a member as appearing to be what it claims to be. Held captures pile up: the assistant requests them, sweeps bring in dozens, bulk uploads add more. DEC-95 already lets the system quietly suggest that a held capture bears on a question; the open part is whether there is also one place to see and clear the backlog.

Example: a sweep of the city's job board brings in 120 near-identical postings. With a list, a member sorts by source, ticks the 120, chooses 'Release together', writes what she sampled and why they are alike, and the record answers per item. Two budget memos a live question relies on are 'crucial': they cannot be ticked for a batch release, and the list says why. Without a list, the postings are released one by one, or never.
alreadySettled: Batch release is legitimate when a collection is large and uniform; each document still gets its own release entry; the member's acknowledgement of uniformity and of what they sampled is recorded; crucial or contested material is never batch-released (Intake Doctrine §4, operator ruling 2026-07-27)
Release is a named member's act, never a machine's (Intake Doctrine §4a)
A held item set aside stays at 'collected' with its reason; there is no route to 'retired' from there by design (Intake Doctrine §8)
Any bulk act: the member chooses, nothing is preselected, each item answers landed or refused with its reason, nothing half-runs silently (Interaction Constructs §S)
No nagging: age may be shown, but nothing is notified unless the member asked (DEC-69; DEC-94)
The bulk release act belongs to ratification (K583); carried to T19

options.label: A
options.name: Held list with bulk triage (as proposed)
options.whatTheMemberSees: A 'Held captures' view, per member and per project, filtered by what they can see. It is sortable by age, source and project, and each row shows its age. Nothing is notified. Ticking several offers: release together (with the uniformity and sampling acknowledgement; crucial items shown as not eligible, with the reason), set aside with one reason, or link to a question.
options.gains: Makes the backlog visible and clearable. The batch rule becomes real instead of theoretical. It matches how sweeps actually fill the record.
options.costs: A visible backlog can feel like a to-do list. Bulk release invites rubber-stamping, and the acknowledgement is the only guard.

options.label: B
options.name: List for seeing, one at a time for acting
options.whatTheMemberSees: The same list, but every release or set-aside is done per capture.
options.gains: Maximum care per document.
options.costs: The 120 postings stay unreleased in practice. It withholds a batch release the doctrine allows.

options.label: C
options.name: No list; held captures surface only where they bear
options.whatTheMemberSees: Held captures appear in search and through DEC-95's quiet suggestions on a question's page. There is no backlog view.
options.gains: Nothing that feels like a queue of chores.
options.costs: Unrelated held captures are never seen. The Intake Doctrine's backlog ceiling becomes invisible to members.

brief.recommendation: Option A, with three guards drawn from standing rules: nothing ticked by default, crucial or contested captures shown but never batch-eligible, and age displayed but never notified. It is the only option that uses the batch release the doctrine already allows, and it keeps the acknowledgement as the honest record of what was checked.
howToAnswer: As recommended.
Option A, but per project only, not per member.
Option C for now; revisit when a group's backlog becomes a problem.
Question first: can a member set aside a batch without giving a reason for each?
brief.ifLeftOpen: Captures are released one by one where a member meets them. The bulk release act exists only in the old store code, and its module move (N400) is already set for T19. Nothing else is blocked.
sources: Intake Doctrine §4 ('What verification asserts, and batch ratification'), §4a, §8

openQuestions.question: How does the queue avoid nagging (DEC-69) while making sure obligations with clocks are not missed?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Respect for members is a requirement; so are deadlines (Operational Principle 3).
openQuestions.context: The queue is the member's one list of 'things that want me', grouped by case (a question or project). It holds obligations (a named person must act, sometimes against a legal deadline), items the record noticed (shown as 'Noticed', K356), and conditions about the product's own machinery. Some obligations carry clocks, such as a records-request response due in so many days.

canonSays.says: 'The workflow must not nag or second-guess members'; repeating, re-confirming and act-detached reminders are the flaw; informing at the act, once, is respect.
'The clock runs. Deadlines are deadlines.'
One standing entry per (member, case), no digest cadence; it 're-notifies only on a snooze increment or when something new lands'. Obligations can never be muted (queue R19, R31).
A passed clock is marked overdue and the action's members are told; the next escalation stage is proposed, never advanced.
Transport (for example email) is undecided; the in-app queue is the only channel.
An undetermined candidate is a lead, never a duty; a record duty is an unmutable obligation for the joined members of every project drawing on either side, leaving only by resolution.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The canon says obligations cannot be muted and overdue clocks are marked, but not how a clock's approach is shown: whether an item's position, colour or wording changes as a deadline nears, and whether anything reaches a member who has not opened the product. DEC-69 forbids repeated reminders, while Operational Principle 3 and monitoring R34 require members to be told; the only sanctioned re-notify triggers are 'snooze ended' and 'something new', and it is undecided whether 'a deadline is now N days away' counts as something new.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The queue lists items by class and case with mute; an overdue clock is shown as an overdue mark on the action's own page; nothing warns of an approaching deadline and nothing leaves the app.

options.option: Treat a clock crossing a stated threshold (for example 'due within 3 days', 'overdue') as a new event: the standing entry rises and says so once per threshold, never repeated.
options.tradeoffs: Uses DEC-10's 'something new' rule without inventing a reminder cadence; needs the thresholds defined (per action kind or profile).

options.option: No escalation of display: sort obligations by due date and show the date; the member judges.
options.tradeoffs: Maximally respectful; a deadline can be missed by a member who does not open the product.

options.option: Add an outside channel (email or push) for clock obligations only, opted into by the member.
options.tradeoffs: Reaches absent members; reopens the transport decision and its security concerns (D-98).

openQuestions.recommendation: Option 1 inside the product, with option 3 left as a member's opt-in later: a threshold is a real change, so it is not nagging.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob: where respect ends and a deadline duty begins is doctrine (DEC-69 is his); the threshold values and look are Design's.

update.note: Not settled. One fixed point is added: a record contradiction is a duty that cannot be muted and leaves the queue only by resolution, while a world one is a lead (DEC-76 item 3; DEC-84 (1)-(2)). Where respect ends and a deadline duty begins remains Bob's.

ruled.decided: A deadline reminder is the member's own request, never the system's nagging: it is set up when the option is chosen in the action plan, from defaults the member sees and can change there, and any further reminder is one the member accepts, perhaps at the system's suggestion. As a deadline nears, the item's position, colour or wording may change; that is display, not a notification. Nothing reaches a member who has not opened the product: no email, push or other outside channel. An overdue deadline notifies once; 'due within N days' is not new unless the member asked for that reminder. An overdue condition's response offers another reminder at a further time, or none (DEC-10). A pushed notice tells once, is dispositionable and ages (DEC-70); the workflow never second-guesses (DEC-69). Threshold looks and wording are Design's.
ruled.title: Reminders without nagging

openQuestions.question: What are the empty and loading states across surfaces, especially long waits (renders deferred, capture requests hours away, statutory clocks of days)?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Canon names waits but no treatment; an empty state can be mistaken for 'nothing to do' or 'could not read'.
openQuestions.context: Many things in the product take time: a capture may take minutes, a page render may be held back ('deferred') with a code, a capture the assistant requested may run hours later when the host allows, and a legal response clock runs for days. Every list can also be empty. What a surface shows while waiting, or when there is nothing, tells the member whether to act, wait or worry.

canonSays.says: 'undetermined' is first-class and must be STATED, 'never invented past and never dressed as an error'; one treatment everywhere: 'what we do not know, and why we do not know it.'
A condition is recorded (no surface), noticed (status where the thing lives) or actionable (a queue item); losing 'noticed' means 'either drowning the member or hiding what is happening'.
A deferred render is held with its code and translation, content 'undetermined'; past its expiry it is released as expired, 'nothing was filed'.
A page that cannot read the group says so, 'never that none is recorded'.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The canon distinguishes 'none' from 'could not read' in one place (the setup page) and defines 'undetermined', but gives no general treatment for empty, loading or long-wait states; the UX substrate marks them 'not specified' on almost every surface. The gap matters because three different truths look alike on screen: nothing exists, the record has not answered yet, and the record answered that it cannot know; plus waits measured in days need a visible 'what happens next and when'.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: Mostly a plain 'Loading…' line and a few empty sentences (for example 'Nothing is waiting for review'); the group name distinguishes none-recorded from could-not-read.

options.option: One product-wide state vocabulary with four named states (nothing here; still reading; could not read, and why; not known, and why) plus a 'waiting on' pattern that names what is awaited, by whom, and the expected or legal date.
options.tradeoffs: Consistent and teachable, matching §U's 'one voice'; needs every surface's reads to tell the four apart, which some plane answers may not yet do.

options.option: Per-surface treatment designed case by case.
options.tradeoffs: Fits each context; drifts, which §U warns teaches members to ignore the signal.

options.option: Option 1 plus an empty state that offers the natural next step for that surface (for example a new project's first step).
options.tradeoffs: Helps newcomers; must not become a prompt that nags (DEC-69).

openQuestions.recommendation: Option 1, adding option 3's next step only where the member has just created the empty thing.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Design: the canon already sets the principle (state it, never dress it as an error); the vocabulary and treatments are detail within it.

brief.settledBy: Part settled: DEC-86 fixes 'Undetermined' and its four neighbours ('Withheld', 'Unrated', 'Nobody looked', 'Refused'), each distinct and never dressed as an error; DEC-94 item 2 rules that as a deadline nears 'the item's position, colour or wording may change … That is display, not a notification'; capture-requests R17, R20, R25 state what a held or expired render says ('nothing was filed'); instance-setup R20 separates 'none' from 'unread'. Still open: a product-wide treatment for empty lists, loading, and long waits.
brief.title: What screens say while waiting or empty
brief.decision: Should every screen use one shared way of saying 'nothing here', 'still loading', 'could not read, and why', and 'waiting on X until date', or should each screen design its own?
brief.whyYours: This could be delegated to Design. The principle is already canon (state gaps, never dress them as errors, Interaction Constructs §U). Bob would still set one thing: whether a long wait must always say what happens next and when, and whether an empty screen may suggest a next step without nagging (DEC-69).
brief.context:
Much in CivicOS takes time. A capture can take minutes. A city site may hold back ('defer') a page render. A capture the assistant asked for may run hours later. A legal response clock (for example, a public-records request) runs for days. And any list can be empty. Three different truths can look identical on screen: nothing exists, the record has not answered yet, and the record answered that it cannot know.

Example: a member asks the assistant to capture the council's agenda page. The city's site defers it. Today the member sees a plain 'Loading…' or a blank list, and may conclude nothing was found. Under a shared pattern she would see: 'Waiting: the city's site asked us to slow down. We will try again after 3:10 pm. Nothing has been filed yet.' On a records request she would see: 'Waiting on the City Clerk's reply, due 14 October (10 days, Gov. Code §7922.535).'

The old interface mostly shows 'Loading…' and a few sentences such as 'Nothing is waiting for review'. Its setup page is the one place that separates 'none recorded' from 'could not read'.
alreadySettled: 'Undetermined' always carries its 'because…' line; four neighbours, each visibly different, none shown as an error (DEC-86; Interaction Constructs §U)
A nearing deadline changes position, colour or wording only; that is display, not a notification; overdue re-notifies once (DEC-94 items 2 and 4)
A deferred render is held with its code and plain explanation, content 'undetermined'; once expired, 'nothing was filed' (capture-requests R17, R20, R25)
A page that cannot read something says so, never that none is recorded (instance-setup R20; Publication §7)
'Alive means live': an open list updates when an item is added or removed, if it does not disrupt (UI-KICKOFF refinements)
Queue items say whose obligation it is: the group's own checkpoint or the counterparty's deadline (Action design PATH.md §3, approved K608)

options.label: A
options.name: One shared vocabulary
options.whatTheMemberSees: Four named states used everywhere: 'Nothing here', 'Still reading', 'Could not read, because…', 'Not known, because…'. Every wait also carries a line naming what is awaited, from whom, and the expected or legal date.
options.gains: Consistent and teachable, matching §U's 'one voice'. A member learns it once.
options.costs: Every screen's data must tell the four apart, and some answers from the record may not yet do so.

options.label: B
options.name: Each screen designed on its own
options.whatTheMemberSees: Wording and look chosen per screen.
options.gains: Fits each context closely.
options.costs: The screens drift apart, and §U warns that inconsistency teaches members to ignore the signal.

options.label: C
options.name: Shared vocabulary plus a next step when empty
options.whatTheMemberSees: As A, and an empty screen offers the natural next step (for example, 'Add the first question' on a new project).
options.gains: Helps newcomers.
options.costs: Risks becoming a prompt that nags (DEC-69).

brief.recommendation: Option A, adding C's next step only on something the member has just created (a new project, a new plan), where the step is information given at the act rather than a nudge. The wording and look can then be delegated to Design.
howToAnswer: As recommended, and leave the rest to Design.
Option A only; no next-step prompts anywhere.
Delegate the whole question to Design.
brief.ifLeftOpen: Design treats each screen as it comes, and 'Loading…' and blank lists persist until the redesign reaches them. Nothing in the build waits.

openQuestions.question: What accessibility level and which languages must the member surfaces and published output meet?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Canon names phones and print only; a civic product's public output may need to reach non-English readers and assistive technology users.
openQuestions.context: The member surfaces are the screens members work in; the published output is the public case page, its print version and its downloadable file, read by residents, journalists, officials and other groups. Accessibility means people using screen readers, keyboards only, magnification or with low vision can use them; language means whether anything appears in languages other than English.

canonSays.says: Devices: phones supported, 'acceptably as a viewing MVP'; the printed publication is 'first-class and must carry the full narrative'.
'The hardening pass' (keyboard and screen-reader coverage) is ABSENT: 'two aria- attributes in 18,736 lines'.
'Accessibility (UX): validate that a static PWA meets Requirement 11', framed as usability for newcomers, not disability access.
Materials must be understandable with no prior civic experience; financial barriers to participation are to be minimized.
The product must serve groups anywhere, not only Oakland.

openQuestions.whyOpen: No canon document names an accessibility standard (such as WCAG 2.2 AA) or any language requirement, for members or for the public. The one 'accessibility' item in the canon means ease of use, not disability access. Language raises a further doctrinal question: a translated published case is not the signed bytes, so who translates, whether a translation is itself published and signed, and how it is marked are all unaddressed.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: English only, almost no screen-reader markup, a narrow-screen viewing layout and a full print layout.

options.option: Adopt WCAG 2.2 AA for member surfaces and published output now; interface language English at first, built so strings can be translated; published cases in the language written.
options.tradeoffs: A recognised bar at modest cost if designed in from the start; non-English readers still depend on the group writing in their language.

options.option: As option 1, plus interface translation per jurisdiction profile (for example Spanish, Chinese, Vietnamese in California) and an optional 'translated rendering' output act, marked as unsigned and naming the signed original.
options.tradeoffs: Reaches the communities most affected; translations become an output act needing doctrine on who stands behind them.

options.option: Defer both to a later hardening pass.
options.tradeoffs: Cheapest now; retrofitting accessibility is costly, and a civic product's public output excluding readers undercuts its mission.

openQuestions.recommendation: Option 1 as a requirement now, with option 2's translated rendering taken up as a separate publication decision.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob: a conformance level and supported languages are requirements, and a translated publication is doctrine; the implementation is Design's.

brief.settledBy: Not settled. No canon, requirement, DEC or K-ruling names an accessibility standard or supported languages (searched the T18 docs, requirements and rulings). DEC-79, DEC-82 and DEC-90 fix three points any standard must honour. jurisdictions R37 'locale' concerns the language of a government's own publications (for capture), not the product's.
brief.title: Accessibility level and languages
brief.decision: Which accessibility standard the member screens and the public case pages must meet, and whether anything appears in languages other than English: the interface, the published case, or both.
brief.whyYours: A conformance level and supported languages are requirements. Whether a translated case is itself published and signed is publication doctrine. The implementation is Design's and BOB's.
brief.context:
The member screens are where members work. The published output is the public case page, its printed version and its downloadable file, read by residents, journalists, officials and other groups. Accessibility means that people using screen readers, only a keyboard, magnification or reduced vision can use them. The widely used benchmark is WCAG 2.2 at level AA. (Note: in CivicOS's own files, 'translation' usually means the plain-English sentence explaining a refusal, not another language.)

Example: a blind resident in East Oakland uses a screen reader to open a published case about sewer fees. Today almost nothing on the page is labelled for her (the old interface has 'two aria- attributes in 18,736 lines'). A Spanish-speaking neighbour sees only English. A member with a tremor who cannot use a mouse cannot open the grade details that appear on hover.

The canon mentions phones (a viewing-first release is acceptable) and a first-class printed case, and Design Requirement 11 asks that materials be usable by newcomers in one session. The only 'accessibility' item in the Technical Architecture means ease of use, not disability access. CivicOS is meant for groups anywhere (K1), so which languages matter depends on the place.
alreadySettled: Every hover has a keyboard-focus or tap equivalent (DEC-79, DEC-82)
Colour is never the only signal: each scale has its icon, each bar its name (DEC-79, DEC-82)
The assistant panel must not trap or lose keyboard focus, one reason it does not float (DEC-90)
Phones supported, acceptably as viewing first; the printed case is first-class and carries the full narrative (UI-KICKOFF refinements)
Materials understandable with no prior civic experience (Design Requirement 11)
No jurisdiction in the product; local facts live in jurisdiction profiles (K1)
The assistant takes typed or spoken input on every surface (Interaction Constructs §P, DEC-27)

options.label: A
options.name: WCAG 2.2 AA now, English first
options.whatTheMemberSees: Everything usable by keyboard and screen reader and readable at 200% zoom and in high contrast. Interface in English, but built so its words can be translated later. Published cases appear in the language the group wrote them in.
options.gains: A recognised bar at modest cost when designed in from the start, not retrofitted. Protects the public page, where readers know least.
options.costs: Non-English readers still depend on the group writing in their language.

options.label: B
options.name: A, plus local languages and translated readings
options.whatTheMemberSees: As A, with the interface offered in the languages a jurisdiction profile names (for example Spanish, Chinese and Vietnamese in California). A group may also issue a 'translated reading' of a case, marked unsigned and naming the signed original.
options.gains: Reaches the communities most affected.
options.costs: A translated case becomes a new output act, needing doctrine on who stands behind the translation and how errors in it are corrected.

options.label: C
options.name: Defer to a later hardening pass
options.whatTheMemberSees: Nothing changes for now.
options.gains: Cheapest today.
options.costs: Retrofitting accessibility is costly, and public output that excludes readers undercuts the mission.

brief.recommendation: Option A as a requirement now. Take up B's translated reading later as its own publication decision, since it raises the question of who signs what.
howToAnswer: As recommended.
Option A, and add Spanish for the interface from the start.
Option B.
Question first: what does AA cost us compared with doing nothing now?
brief.ifLeftOpen: The redesign proceeds with only the three ruled points (focus or tap for hover, no colour-only signals, no focus traps). Every screen built meanwhile may need rework to meet a standard chosen later.

openQuestions.question: How does a subject named in a case (an office, or an official in role) see and respond, and how is the publisher's right-of-reply declaration shown?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Right of reply is a declaration, not a gate (DEC-13); a response returns as captured evidence, not a channel.
openQuestions.context: A published case often names a subject: a government office, or an official acting in their role. Good practice is to put the findings to the subject before publishing and report what came back. The subject meets the product only as any reader does, on the public case page; the publishing group records whether it sought the subject's comment and why.

canonSays.says: 'The subject's right of reply is a declaration, not a gate': the publisher's determination and justification are an element of the group's recorded bias.
Pre-publication contact with the subject is the required workflow in practice literature, overturning its earlier listing as a hazard.
Every case must state a subject position, one of 'sought_and_answered', 'sought_no_answer', 'not_sought', and a subject justification.
A 'request_for_comment' action must name an inquiry and a clock entry; a reply is captured bytes or a member's account, and 'a non-response is recorded with its date'.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The record side is built; the experience is not. Undecided: how a reader and the subject see the three-valued position and its justification (prominence, wording, whether a reply is linked to where it is quoted); whether a subject can find cases naming them; and how a reply that arrives after publication shows up (it can only enter as captured evidence and appear in a later edition). The tension is between the practice literature calling contact 'required' and the canon refusing to make it a gate.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The published case prints 'Position on putting this case to its subject' with the justification; the review copy shows it; a reply box for subjects was considered and refused.
related: 17 (a reply leads to a new edition)
19 (position is part of the recorded bias)

options.option: Show the subject position prominently near the top of every published case in plain words ('We asked the Office of X on date; they replied / did not reply by date / we did not ask, because…'), each linked to the captured correspondence where public.
options.tradeoffs: Fair and self-evident; linking correspondence needs a rule on which correspondence is published as evidence.

options.option: Add a public 'cases naming this subject' index keyed on the subject registry.
options.tradeoffs: Lets offices find and answer cases; it also creates a listing of targets, which may read as adversarial.

options.option: Keep it where it is (a line among the completeness details).
options.tradeoffs: No new work; a reader may miss it, weakening the fairness it records.

openQuestions.recommendation: Option 1: it makes the declaration legible without making it a gate; revisit option 2 when there is a directory.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob for prominence and any subject-facing index (effects on people outside the project); Design for wording and layout.

brief.settledBy: The record side is settled and partly built: Publication §3 rule 6 (DEC-13) 'The subject's right of reply is a declaration, not a gate'; case-authoring R3 requires a subject position (sought and answered / sought, no answer / not sought) and a justification, fresh each edition (R10); actions R44 (K603) makes a request for comment name the questions put and a response window, 'the window's length never enforced'; actions R34 records a reply as captured bytes or a member's account, and a non-response with its date. DEC-77 and DEC-84 (10) fix what a named office reads in an obligation-against-act finding ('cause not established' unless evidenced). K590 (D1): addressees are never a private individual. Open: how prominently and in what words the position is shown, whether a reply is linked, a subject-facing index, and a reply that arrives after publication.
brief.title: How the subject of a case sees it and replies
brief.decision: How prominently a published case shows whether the group put its findings to the subject (the office or official named) and what came back; whether the replies are linked; whether offices can find cases naming them; and what happens when a reply arrives after publication.
brief.whyYours: It affects people outside the group, the offices a case names, and how fair the product looks. Prominence and any public index of subjects are Bob's. Wording and layout are Design's.
brief.context:
A published case often names a 'subject': a government office, or an official acting in their role (never a private individual, K590). Good practice is to put the findings to the subject before publishing and report what came back. CivicOS makes this a declaration, not a gate: every case says whether the subject was asked, answered, or not asked, and why. A reply is recorded as captured evidence or a member's account; a reply box for subjects was considered and refused.

Example: the group sends the Public Works director a request for comment on 1 October with a 10-day window. No answer comes; the case publishes on 15 October. Today the page lists 'Position on putting this case to its subject' among the completeness details, where a reader could miss it. On 20 October the director emails a reply, and nothing tells the group its published edition now has an answer it did not include.
alreadySettled: Right of reply is a declaration, not a gate, and part of the group's recorded bias (Publication §3 rule 6; DEC-13)
Every case states one of three positions with a justification, authored fresh each edition (case-authoring R3, R10)
A request for comment names the questions put and states a response window; the window's length is never enforced (actions R44; K603)
Replies are captured bytes or a member's account; a non-response is recorded with its date (actions R34)

For a finding that a duty and the government's act diverge: Criteria and Condition as facts; Cause only when evidenced, else 'cause not established'; Recommendation a proposed action, never a policy position (DEC-77 item 2; DEC-84 (10))
Addressees are offices and roles, never a private individual (K590, D1)
Pressure against the group is recorded as evidence (K597 (1))

options.label: A
options.name: Plain-words box near the top
options.whatTheMemberSees: Near the top of every published case: 'We asked the Director of Public Works on 1 October, giving 10 days. No reply had arrived by 15 October.' Or: 'We did not ask, because…'. Where the group chose to publish the correspondence as evidence, it is linked.
options.gains: Fair and self-evident, and it stays a declaration, not a gate.
options.costs: Linking needs a rule on which correspondence becomes public evidence (the group's choice at publishing).

options.label: B
options.name: A, plus a public index of subjects
options.whatTheMemberSees: As A, and a public page 'Cases naming the Department of Public Works'.
options.gains: Offices can find and answer cases about them.
options.costs: Builds a public list of targets, which may read as adversarial. It also needs a directory that does not exist yet.

options.label: C
options.name: Leave it among the completeness details
options.whatTheMemberSees: As today.
options.gains: No new work.
options.costs: Readers miss it, weakening the fairness the record captures.

brief.recommendation: Option A. Revisit B when a directory exists. For a late reply, my recommendation is that a reply recorded against a request for comment after its case was published puts a notice in the owning project's queue ('The Director replied after edition 1'), prompting a later edition. This follows DEC-84 (13)'s pattern for a tension found after publication. It is not yet a rule.
howToAnswer: As recommended, including the late-reply notice.
Option A, but never link correspondence.
Option B now.
Question first: can a subject ask us to publish their reply in full?
brief.ifLeftOpen: Published cases keep the position as one line among the completeness details, and a late reply is found only if a member looks at the action.
sources: Action design MATRIX.md 'Record replies and outcomes'

openQuestions.question: How is a correction made visible to people who relied on an earlier edition (pull, never push)?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Media and peers rely on cases; a published hash answers forever.
openQuestions.context: A published case can never be changed or withdrawn. When a group finds an error or new evidence, it publishes a new edition; the old one stays readable forever at the same address and fingerprint. Journalists, officials and other groups may have quoted or cited the earlier edition. 'Pull, never push' means the product lets readers find out about a correction but never sends them a message.

canonSays.says: A published case is revised as a new edition, 'treated as a separate document; a citation names an edition; supersession is surfaced, not followed'.
Nothing updates or deletes a published row; 'a correction is a new edition, and an edition answers forever'.
The exclusion statement, subject justification and bias acknowledgement must be freshly authored for each edition.
Inside the group, a finding citing an older edition gains an 'edition' re-evaluation cause when a later edition exists.
'NOTIFY ME. Refused': it converts a reader into a list; the editions index and a held hash tell a reader what to check.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The canon guarantees that later editions are findable but nothing requires the new edition to say what was corrected and why; the freshness rule covers the exclusion statement and bias acknowledgement, not a correction note. Also undecided: how prominently an older edition announces it has been superseded, and how a reader in another group, who holds only a citation, learns of it without a central directory.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: Every edition page shows a banner, 'A newer edition of this case exists', with links, stating the old one still answers and that its numbers are its own; the published index lists all editions.

options.option: Require an authored 'What changed in this edition' statement on every edition after the first, shown at the top of the new edition and quoted in the older edition's banner.
options.tradeoffs: Gives readers the correction in one place; one more authored field at publication, which must not be a pro-forma box.

options.option: Generate a machine difference between editions (findings added, removed, strength changed) beside the banner.
options.tradeoffs: Objective and effortless; does not explain why, and a diff can overstate trivial changes.

options.option: Keep the banner and index only.
options.tradeoffs: Already built; a reader sees that something changed but not what or why.

openQuestions.recommendation: Option 1 with option 2 as supporting detail: corrections should explain themselves, and the pull model stays intact.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob: a new required authored statement at publication is a requirement; banner design is Design's.

brief.settledBy: Not settled. Settled around it: DEC-12 (a correction is a new edition; 'supersession is surfaced, not followed'); publication R24 ('a correction is a new edition, and an edition answers forever'); case-authoring R10 (statement, subject justification, exclusions and bias acknowledgement authored fresh each edition); reevaluation R2 ('edition' cause inside the group); DEC-84 (13) (a tension found after publication is disclosed or resolved in a later edition); DEC-94 item 3 (no outside channel). Nothing requires a new edition to say what changed and why.
brief.title: How a correction reaches people who relied on the old edition
brief.decision: Should every new edition carry an authored 'What changed in this edition' statement, shown on it and on the old edition's banner, and how should readers elsewhere learn a newer edition exists without CivicOS ever sending them a message?
brief.whyYours: A new required statement at publishing is a requirement and adds to the signing ceremony. How the product treats people who relied on a case is doctrine (pull, never push). The banner's design is Design's.
brief.context:
A published case can never be changed or withdrawn. To correct it, the group publishes a new edition, and the old one stays readable forever at the same address and fingerprint. Journalists, officials and other groups may have quoted the earlier one. 'Pull, never push' means readers can find out about a correction but CivicOS never sends them a message. A 'notify me' feature was considered and refused, because it turns readers into a mailing list.

Example: edition 1 of a case says the city moved $4.2M out of the sewer fund. A member finds a double-counted transfer, and edition 2 says $3.1M. A reporter who quoted edition 1 opens the link a month later. The old interface shows a banner: 'A newer edition of this case exists', with a link. The reporter still has to compare the two by hand to learn what changed and why. Another group that cited edition 1 learns nothing unless someone looks.

The freshness rule already forces four fields to be re-written each edition, but none of them is a note about the correction.
alreadySettled: Editions are separate documents; a citation names an edition; supersession is surfaced, not followed (DEC-12; Publication §2)
Nothing updates or deletes a published row; each edition answers forever (publication R24)
The statement, subject justification, exclusions and bias acknowledgement are authored fresh each edition (case-authoring R10)
Inside the group, a finding citing an older edition gets an 'edition' re-evaluation notice (reevaluation R2)
A tension found after publication leaves the signed edition as it is; a later edition discloses or resolves it (DEC-84 (13))
No email, push or other outside channel (DEC-94 item 3); 'notify me' was refused (old UI note H2)
A correction is always a further named, dated act; the reader can see both (Interaction Constructs §A, DEC-19)

options.label: A
options.name: Authored 'What changed' statement
options.whatTheMemberSees: Signing edition 2 asks for 'What changed in this edition, and why' (for example, 'Corrected a double-counted $1.1M transfer; the finding stands at a lower figure'). It leads edition 2, and edition 1's banner quotes it.
options.gains: Readers get the correction and its reason in one place, in the group's own words.
options.costs: One more field at signing, which must not become a boilerplate box.

options.label: B
options.name: Machine difference only
options.whatTheMemberSees: Beside the banner, a computed list: findings added or removed, strength changed, documents added.
options.gains: Objective and effortless.
options.costs: Says what changed but never why, and can make trivial changes look large.

options.label: C
options.name: Banner and index only
options.whatTheMemberSees: As today.
options.gains: Already built.
options.costs: Readers see that something changed but not what or why.

brief.recommendation: Option A, with B's computed list shown beneath it as supporting detail, labelled 'Machine work'. Corrections should explain themselves, and the pull model stays intact. For readers in another group, my recommendation is that a group's CivicOS treats the published index of any group it cites as a watched source. A newer edition then raises the same 'edition' notice inside the citing group. That is still pull: its own instance looks, and nobody is messaged.
howToAnswer: As recommended.
Option A, without the machine list.
As recommended, but don't watch other groups' indexes yet.
Question first: must the statement be fresh even for a minor typo fix?
brief.ifLeftOpen: New editions publish with the banner and index only. The ceremony (DEC-80) is being designed now, so adding a field later means reworking its 'the edition this creates' step.

openQuestions.question: How is attribution chosen and shown (group, project, cover, name), including off-the-record sources, without making pseudonymous work look weaker?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Attribution surface is designed in Program B and unbuilt; an identity badge would be a structural prior against a class of publisher.
openQuestions.context: When a member's own firsthand observation (something they saw or heard, recorded in their words) is used in a published case, that member chooses how they are credited: as the group, the project, their cover (a name an administrator gave them), or by name. A source who spoke to the member off the record can be included without any field that could identify them. The worry is that anything short of a real name should not look like weaker evidence.

canonSays.says: Attribution is the attesting member's choice among group, project, cover or name; an off-the-record source is valid.
The attribution surface is 'designed in Program B and rowed nowhere yet'.

No default; chosen per case edition and observation; an unchosen observation blocks ratifying that edition, and 'name' publishes the handle (both provisional, with Bob). Testimony keeps its own grade whatever the level (§3).

canonSays.source: publication R17, R39 (R39 not yet met, K240)
canonSays.says: The plane records the choice with refusals for invalid levels; the level in force is read per case edition.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The record rules and the act exist; how the choice is made and shown does not. Undecided: where the author is asked (their own queue item, or the case draft), how the three blocking consequences of not choosing are explained without pressure, and how the public page renders 'group' or 'cover' so it reads as a protection, not as missing credibility. Two provisionals are still with Bob: that an unchosen observation blocks ratification, and that 'name' means the handle.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: Nothing: no attribution act is offered, and the published page names each finding's attesting member id.

options.option: Ask in the author's queue as an obligation when a draft first reaches their observation, offering the four levels with one sentence each on what the public will see; show every level publicly in the same neutral style with the testimony grade beside it.
options.tradeoffs: Respects DEC-69 (asked once, at the act) and keeps the grade the visible measure of strength; adds an obligation that can hold up a case.

options.option: As option 1, but the case owner can publish without that finding while waiting.
options.tradeoffs: Already the canon's recourse; making it visible on the draft avoids pressure on the author.

options.option: Default to 'group' with the author able to change it.
options.tradeoffs: Never blocks; contradicts the ruling that there is no default.

openQuestions.recommendation: Option 1 with option 2's recourse shown on the draft; confirm the two provisionals with Bob first.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob for the two provisionals (blocking and handle-as-name, both doctrine about members' own words); Design for the choice screen and uniform public display.

brief.settledBy: Much is settled: Publication §3 rule 7 (four levels, the attesting member's choice, off-the-record sources valid); DEC-88 (choosing attribution is high friction, a full dialog stating the name becomes permanent at publication); DEC-78 item 5 and K509 (4) (a source's identity is a dated history; the group is never first to make a source more public; a case shows 'an unnamed source' unless consented). The two MEMBER-KNOWLEDGE-DESIGN provisionals are built and sit inside requirements Bob approved 'as recommended, for now' on 2026-09-26 (K102): ratification R2/R18 refuse ratifying while an observation is unchosen (ATTRIBUTION_UNCHOSEN, C-92.10), and publication R17 refuses 'name' with no handle (C-92.9). Neither was put to him as its own question, and the UX substrate still lists both as Bob's.
brief.title: How members choose how they are credited
brief.decision: Confirm two built rules: (1) a case edition cannot be signed while a member whose observation it uses has not chosen how to be credited; (2) 'by name' publishes the member's chosen handle, not a legal name. Then approve how the choice is asked and shown.
brief.whyYours: Both rules concern members' control over their own words and identity. That is doctrine, and they are marked for Bob. The choice screen and the public look are Design's once he confirms.
brief.context:
An 'observation' is something a member saw or heard, recorded in their own words and signed. When a case uses one, that member chooses how they are credited: the group, the project, their cover (a name an administrator gave them), or by name. There is no default, and the observation keeps its own testimony grade whatever the level, so anything short of a name must not look weaker. The record keeps no legal names (Membership v2 §3).

Example: a case draft rests on Maria's observation at a pump station. Maria gets a queue item: 'Your observation is used in "Sewer overflows, edition 1". How should you be credited?', with four choices, each saying what the public will see. Choosing 'by name' opens a full dialog saying her handle 'mgarcia' becomes permanent at publication. Until she chooses, the owner cannot sign that edition; the owner's recourse is to drop the finding resting on her words. On the public page, 'Credited to the group' sits in the same neutral style as a name, with the testimony grade beside it.
alreadySettled: Four levels, chosen by the member, per case edition and observation; off-the-record sources valid (Publication §3 rule 7; MEMBER-KNOWLEDGE-DESIGN §4)
No default; never prefilled (MEMBER-KNOWLEDGE-DESIGN §4)
High friction: a full dialog stating that the name becomes permanent at publication (DEC-88)
Testimony keeps its own grade whatever the credit level (MEMBER-KNOWLEDGE-DESIGN §3)

Sources: the group is never first to make a source more public; consent asked at publishing and stated as permanent; 'known to the group, not recorded' is first-class (DEC-78 item 5); a case shows 'an unnamed source' unless consented (K509 (4))
Built and in approved requirements 'for now': unchosen blocks signing (ratification R2, R18, C-92.10); 'name' needs a handle (publication R17, C-92.9) (K102)

options.label: A
options.name: Keep both rules; ask in the author's queue
options.whatTheMemberSees: As in the example: the author is asked once, in their queue, when a draft first uses their observation. The owner's draft shows 'waiting on Maria's choice, or publish without this finding'. Every level appears publicly in one neutral style, with the grade beside it.
options.gains: Each member controls their own words, the owner has an honest way forward, and the grade stays the visible measure of strength.
options.costs: One member's silence can hold up one finding.

options.label: B
options.name: Credit the group if no choice is made
options.whatTheMemberSees: If Maria does not answer, her observation publishes as 'the group'.
options.gains: Never holds a case up.
options.costs: Contradicts 'no default' and publishes a member's words without their choice.

options.label: C
options.name: 'By name' means a typed legal name
options.whatTheMemberSees: Choosing 'by name' asks for the name to print, stored only in the signed case.
