openQuestions.question: How are declared bias statements shown to readers so that a lens is weighable, not a weapon (the two-audience choice)?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Opponents will quote the manifest; the malformedness rule makes it survivable only if shown well.
openQuestions.context: A group declares its 'bias': a set of written statements about how it treats certain sources (for example 'claims by X must be cross-checked'), each with a justification. Every published case carries the bias in force when it was produced (the 'manifest') and an acknowledgement the publisher wrote about what that lens did to this edition's findings. Opponents will read and quote it; the aim is that a reader can weigh the lens, and it cannot easily be turned against the group.

canonSays.source: Declared Bias 'The two-audience choice, made knowingly'
canonSays.says: 'Published work carries its bias manifest, and opponents will quote it'; the trade is accepted because a declared, justified rule is more respectable than an undeclared lens, and 'the malformedness rule is what makes each statement survivable when read aloud by an adversary'.
Statements may raise scrutiny, constrain inference or assert evidenced patterns; they 'may never issue verdicts' ('X lies' is refused).

canonSays.source: Declared Bias 'The bias acknowledgement, authored at export' (DEC-46, DEC-20)
canonSays.says: The manifest (computed, hashed) and the acknowledgement (authored, fresh per edition) travel together; a disclosure, 'never a bar'.
Members and public readers read the lens in force.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The doctrine accepts that the manifest will be quoted but says nothing about how it is presented: where it sits on the case, whether justifications and citations are shown with each statement, whether the acknowledgement leads, and how the three statement kinds are explained to a lay reader. A statement quoted without its justification is exactly the 'weapon' reading the doctrine wants to avoid, so the display is load-bearing.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The public case page shows under 'Declared bias' only each finding's hunch legs ('none declared'), not the manifest's statements or the publisher's acknowledgement, which appear only on the review copy.

options.option: A 'The lens this was produced under' section: the publisher's acknowledgement first, then each statement shown with its kind in plain words, its justification and citations inseparable from its text, plus a short explanation of why the group declares bias.
options.tradeoffs: Makes each statement quotable only with its reasons; longer page, handled by progressive disclosure and full print.

options.option: A compact summary (counts by kind, subjects named) linking to the full manifest.
options.tradeoffs: Clean first view; a summary line naming a subject without its justification is the easiest thing to quote out of context.

options.option: Show the manifest only in the downloadable file.
options.tradeoffs: Least exposure; contradicts DEC-20's 'public and accompanies every published case'.

openQuestions.recommendation: Option 1: pairing every statement with its justification is what makes the two-audience choice survivable, and it fixes the old page's mislabelled 'Declared bias'.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Design within the doctrine (DEC-20, DEC-46 and the two-audience choice already decide that it is shown); Bob only if the summary-first form is preferred.

brief.settledBy: Not settled; no ruling since the substrate touches the display. Settled around it: DEC-20 (bias is public and accompanies every published case); DEC-46 (the acknowledgement is authored by the publisher at export, 'not a pre-check checkbox'); the manifest is stamped into every case document (D-84; case-authoring R15 answers `bias_manifest`); the malformedness rule and the two-audience choice (Declared Bias).
brief.title: How a group's declared bias appears to the public
brief.decision: On a published case, is the group's declared lens shown in full, with each statement bound to its justification and the publisher's acknowledgement first, or as a compact summary that links to the full list?
brief.whyYours: Mostly Design's: DEC-20 and DEC-46 already decide that it is shown. Bob decides only whether the full form is required on the public page. That choice sets how the group faces opponents who will quote it, which the Declared Bias doctrine treats as a deliberate trade.
brief.context:
A group declares its 'bias': a short set of written rules about how it treats certain sources, each with a justification. There are three kinds. 'Scrutiny': claims from this source must be cross-checked. 'Inference': for example, silence from the city attorney is not agreement. 'Pattern': an evidenced claim about how an institution behaves, which must cite evidence. Rules that issue verdicts ('X lies') are refused. Every published case carries the lens in force (the 'manifest') and the publisher's own acknowledgement of what that lens did to this edition.

Example: a council member's staffer finds a case and posts: 'This group says the Auditor controls the narrative.' If the page shows that line alone, it reads as an accusation. If it shows the full statement ('Pattern: the Auditor uses its discretion to control the narrative, which limits identified remediation options') with its justification and three cited audit reports, the quote carries its reasons.

Today the old public page shows under 'Declared bias' only each finding's hunches ('none declared'). The manifest and acknowledgement appear only on the private review copy, so the label is misleading.
alreadySettled: The bias is public and accompanies every published case (DEC-20)
The acknowledgement is authored by the publisher at export and fresh each edition (DEC-46; case-authoring R10)
The manifest is computed, hashed and stamped into the signed case document (D-84; case-authoring R15, R22)
Statements may raise scrutiny, constrain inference or assert evidenced patterns, never verdicts; pattern statements must cite (Declared Bias 'The malformedness rule', 'Statement kinds')
The trade is accepted knowingly: opponents will quote it (Declared Bias 'The two-audience choice')

options.label: A
options.name: Full lens, reasons attached
options.whatTheMemberSees: A section 'The lens this was produced under'. It starts with the publisher's acknowledgement, then each statement with its kind in plain words, its justification and its citations kept together, and a two-line note on why the group declares bias. Collapsible on screen, printed in full.
options.gains: No statement can be copied without its reasons in view. It also fixes the old page's mislabelled section.
options.costs: A longer page, handled by collapsing on screen and full text in print.

options.label: B
options.name: Summary first
options.whatTheMemberSees: '3 declared rules: 1 scrutiny, 1 inference, 1 pattern, naming the Auditor', linking to the full list.
options.gains: Clean first view.
options.costs: A summary line naming a subject without its reasons is the easiest thing to quote out of context.

options.label: C
options.name: Only in the downloadable file
options.whatTheMemberSees: Nothing on the page; the manifest is in the signed download.
options.gains: Least exposure.
options.costs: Contradicts DEC-20's 'public and accompanies every published case' in spirit.

brief.recommendation: Option A. Keeping every statement with its justification is what makes the two-audience choice survivable, as the doctrine intends.
howToAnswer: As recommended.
Option A, but put the section after the findings, not before.
Leave it to Design within DEC-20.

openQuestions.question: How are hunches shown during investigation (temporary high grade) versus in strength (inert), and how is clearing one before publication presented?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: A hunch inflates a grade; a case over an uncleared hunch states a strength that is not true.
openQuestions.context: A hunch is a member's own declared guess that two pieces of evidence are connected before the record can prove it. While a group is still investigating, the hunch lets it tie together material that otherwise would not link up. Before a case is published every hunch must be cleared: the case has to stand on its own without it. Members meet it on evidence legs, the strength panel and at publishing.

canonSays.source: DEC-15 (Declared Bias, 'a HUNCH is temporary declared bias')
canonSays.says: A hunch gets 'a temporary high enough grade' to bring disconnected evidence together; 'a published case must pass... without any hunch connections.'
Visible as a hunch 'on every surface'; clearing means 'the case must still hold when the hunch is removed'; 'During open it composes normally'.
A hunch leg is inert in every strength pair whatever grade it states, and is always named as a hunch.
Only hunch debt blocks publication, refused by name UNCLEARED_HUNCH; ordinary bias debt is disclosed.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The canon gives a hunch two jobs that pull apart. The Declared Bias text says a hunch 'composes normally' while a question is open, so its grade does count; strength R5, approved by Bob on 2026-09-26 (K102), makes it count for nothing in every strength figure. The design must say where the temporary grade is visible and useful if strength ignores it. Clearing also has no screen: the preflight (REC-15) is deferred by DEC-33.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: It marks a hunch leg 'HUNCH' with author and date and warns on the strength panel that the case cannot publish; strength counts the hunch.
related: Q5 grades in the project workspace
Q20 declared bias shown to readers

options.option: Two readings side by side: the leg shows its hunch grade in an unmistakable hunch style for linking, and the strength panel shows the pair without hunches plus a line 'N hunches not counted'.
options.tradeoffs: Honest and teaches the rule; a second number could confuse.

options.option: A clearing checklist before publish listing every hunch leg with its two ways out: earn a real grade, or show the case still holds without it.
options.tradeoffs: Makes clearing a concrete task; needs a placeholder until the DEC-33 ceremony exists.

openQuestions.recommendation: Combine the first and third: show the hunch grade only on the leg, keep strength hunch-free with the count named, and list hunches as a to-do before publishing. Bob should confirm strength R5 overrides the 'composes normally' sentence.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob for the one doctrinal point (whether a hunch counts in any strength figure while open, R5 versus the Declared Bias text); Design for the visual treatment and the clearing list.

brief.settledBy: Partly settled. strength R5 ('A leg whose grade source is hunch is inert in every pair, whatever grade it states … always named as a hunch') was approved by Bob 'as recommended, for now' (K102), and K187 reads it whole (a hunch contributes nothing). Clearing is settled in substance: case-authoring R12 refuses UNCLEARED_HUNCH, and DEC-80 item 3 lands it in the ceremony's pre-flight before the first screen, naming every leg (C-120.7). Still unreconciled: Declared Bias still says 'During open it composes normally', and nothing says where the hunch's temporary grade does its job if strength ignores it.
brief.title: What a hunch's grade does, and clearing it
brief.decision: Confirm that a hunch's temporary grade exists only to connect evidence while investigating and never counts in strength, and correct the Declared Bias sentence that says otherwise. Then approve how hunches are shown and listed for clearing before publishing.
brief.whyYours: Whether a hunch counts in any strength figure is doctrine, and it is Bob's own DEC-15 in tension with a requirement he approved 'for now'. The visual treatment and the clearing list are Design's.
brief.context:
A 'hunch' is a member's declared guess that two pieces of evidence are connected before the record can show it. Bob's DEC-15 gives it 'a temporary high enough grade' so that otherwise disconnected evidence can be related while investigating. It must be cleared before publishing: the case has to stand without it. 'Strength' is the pair of letter grades (capture and connection) showing how easily someone else could check an answer. The workspace now shows it for every question (DEC-82).

The tension is between two texts. Declared Bias says a hunch 'composes normally' during investigation, meaning its grade counts. Strength R5 makes it count for nothing in every strength figure, so that the strength a member sees is never inflated by a guess.

Example: a member suspects the contractor on two invoices is the same firm under two names. She links them as a hunch graded B. The question page shows the link in a distinct hunch style: 'Hunch (B) · Maria · 2 Oct'. The two invoices now appear together in searches and suggestions. The strength badges beside the question read '[capture B] [connection C] · 1 hunch not counted'. At publishing, the pre-flight lists the hunch before the first screen with its two ways out: earn a real grade from evidence, or show the case holds without it.
alreadySettled: A hunch is temporary declared bias with a grade, visible as a hunch on every surface from the moment it is made (DEC-15; Declared Bias)
Only hunch debt blocks publication; other bias is disclosed (DEC-20; Publication §3 rule 4)
Hunch inert in strength, always named (strength R5; K102 'for now'; K187)
Uncleared hunch refused before the first screen of the ceremony, each leg named (case-authoring R12, C-120.7; DEC-80 item 3)
Strength shown as two badges, never one score; 'Unrated' and 'Undetermined' named (DEC-82; DEC-86)
Theme hunches are proposals kept apart from members until a member places them (connections R41, R44, R48)

options.label: A
options.name: Links, never counts
options.whatTheMemberSees: As in the example. The hunch's grade appears only on the link, in hunch style, and lets evidence be connected and found together. Strength ignores it and says how many hunches it left out. A 'Hunches to clear' list sits on the question page and in the pre-flight.
options.gains: Honest strength at all times. Teaches the rule. Matches the approved requirement.
options.costs: Two readings sit side by side (the hunch's letter and the strength that ignores it), which needs clear styling.

options.label: B
options.name: Counts while investigating
options.whatTheMemberSees: Two strength readings: 'with hunches' and 'without hunches'.
options.gains: Literal to 'composes normally'. Shows what the case would be if the hunch proves true.
options.costs: Strength R5 must change. A 'with hunches' pair can be quoted as real strength.

options.label: C
options.name: Hunches carry no grade
options.whatTheMemberSees: A hunch is a plain dashed link with no letter.
options.gains: Simplest.
options.costs: Contradicts DEC-15 ('the grade is the point').

brief.recommendation: Option A. Confirm R5 over the 'composes normally' sentence, which BOB then corrects in Declared Bias. The hunch's grade still does DEC-15's job of bringing evidence together, just not inside strength.
howToAnswer: As recommended.
Option A, but hide the hunch letter too and show only 'hunch'.
Option B.
Question first: does a hunch still let the assistant treat the two documents as connected?
brief.ifLeftOpen: Strength R5 stays approved 'for now' and is not yet met (the live code still counts a hunch at its stated grade), and the canon keeps two contradicting sentences, so the workspace's strength badges could be built on one reading and questioned under the other.
sources: Declared Bias 'RULED 2026-08-01: a HUNCH is temporary declared bias'

openQuestions.question: What does a group see when it names its cases for audiences with different standards of proof (journalist vs lawyer), given the catalogue of standards by audience is owed?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Without it the project bar is 'a number a project picks'.
openQuestions.context: Every published case is held to a 'bar': the standard of evidence it must meet, declared on the project that publishes it. A journalist's project and a lawyer's project may use the same findings but need different bars. The owner declares it at setup; readers see it beside the strength each finding reached.

canonSays.says: 'The bar... is a property of a project, not an inquiry or claim.' Nothing composes across projects: one finding may clear a journalist project's bar and fall short of a lawyer project's, 'and both facts stand.'
The CATALOGUE OF STANDARDS by audience and output act is owed; 'without it required_strength is a number a project picks.'
Eight audiences are the professional roles; differences between them belong to the output act (certification, persistence, addressing), never to a field on the case.

An undeclared axis is stated in words ('no bar set on the ... axis'), never a default; the group default seeds new projects and gates nothing; only an active administrator may set it (R15, not yet met).

openQuestions.whyOpen: The mechanism exists but the content does not: there is no catalogue telling a group what grade a journalist, a court or an auditor actually expects, so the setup screen can only offer bare letters A-D. The Publication table still says 'strictest wins' for the bar while DEC-72 removed composition across projects, a leftover a designer could misread. Certification and persistence differences between audiences are also 'unmade'.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The old interface only displays the bar on a published case (declared, or 'none was declared' with the explanation that an absent bar is not a bar of zero); it offers no screen to declare one.

options.option: Ship the bar chooser with letters and plain-language meanings only, and a visible note that audience guidance is not yet available.
options.tradeoffs: Buildable now and honest; groups still pick a number without guidance.

options.option: Commission the catalogue first (research per audience and output act), then design the chooser around audience presets.
options.tradeoffs: Gives the guidance the canon wants; delays the screen and needs research Bob must scope.

openQuestions.recommendation: Build the first option now, since the bar already works, and put the catalogue on Bob's list as a research item with a named trigger; the chooser gains presets when it lands.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob: the catalogue is a requirements and doctrine question (what standard each audience needs); Design settles the chooser's wording within it.

brief.settledBy: Partly. DEC-81 (1): 'a CO-ATTESTED Grade B ... is sufficient to publish'; Grade A stays 'the ceiling for adversarial or legal use' (deferred, DEC-81 (4)). For actions, not publication: 'the venue sets the standard of evidence: no action is refused for its grade' (K597 (3), K600 (b)), with each venue's standard held as sourced data in the jurisdiction profile (jurisdictions R39) and shown beside each exhibit's grade (filings R25). Still open: Publication §7 and §9's table, 'the catalogue of standards by audience and output act ... OWED ... does not exist'.
brief.title: Standards of proof by audience (the project's bar)
brief.decision: Should projects set their bar now from plain letters, with an honest note that no audience guidance exists yet? And when guidance does come, should it take the form Bob just approved for legal venues: sourced facts in the group's jurisdiction profile, reading 'undetermined' where nobody has measured them?
brief.whyYours: What standard of proof a newsroom, a court or an auditor expects is doctrine and requirements. Publication §7 calls it owed research, and commissioning research is a scope call. Design only words the chooser within what Bob sets.
context: A project is a group's line of work toward a stated goal. A case is the argued product a project publishes. Every project may declare a 'bar': the minimum strength each finding the case relies on must reach. The bar covers two separate axes, capture (how well the documents are held) and connection (how firmly the links between them are established), each graded A to D. Readers see the bar beside the strength each finding reached.

The mechanism works, but the guidance does not exist. Publication §7: 'without it required_strength is a number a project picks.' Example: a group opens one project to support a reporter's story and another to hand a complaint to a lawyer. The setup screen offers letters A to D on each axis. Nothing tells the owner what either audience actually expects.

Since then Bob settled two nearby points: co-attested Grade B is enough to publish (DEC-81), and for actions each venue's standard is recorded, with its source, in the jurisdiction profile, shown beside every exhibit's grade and flagged when an exhibit falls short, but never blocking (K597, K600). That is a ready-made pattern for publication audiences.
alreadySettled: The bar belongs to a project and never combines across projects; one finding may clear one project's bar and miss another's, 'and both facts stand' (DEC-72 (1); strength R14).

The group default seeds new projects and gates nothing, and only an active administrator may set it (strength R15, not yet built). Setting it is one of the six high-friction acts, with a full dialog (DEC-88 (4)).
Differences between audiences belong to the output act, never to a field on the case (Publication §6).
For actions, a venue's standard is sourced profile data, 'undetermined' when absent, and never blocks (K597 (3), K600 (b), jurisdictions R39, filings R25).

options.label: A
options.name: Letters now, with an honest note
options.whatTheMemberSees: The owner picks a letter per axis, each with a one-line meaning (for example 'B: an outsider can check the copy and when it existed'), under the line 'There is no guidance yet on what particular audiences expect.'
options.gains: Can be built now, and it is honest.
options.costs: Groups still guess.

options.label: B
options.name: Audience standards as sourced profile facts
options.whatTheMemberSees: The same chooser, plus 'Newspaper publication: B/C (source: ...)' (illustrative) where the profile holds a sourced standard, and 'Undetermined: nobody has measured what this audience expects' where it does not. The owner still decides.
options.gains: Reuses the pattern Bob approved for venues, grows per jurisdiction, and is never a silent default.
options.costs: Needs research and a requirement, and starts nearly empty.

options.label: C
options.name: Research first; the chooser waits
options.whatTheMemberSees: No bar chooser until the catalogue exists; a project's bar reads 'none declared'.
options.gains: Guidance from day one.
options.costs: Delays the screen, and the research scope is Bob's to set.

brief.recommendation: Build A now, and name B as the form guidance will take: it mirrors what Bob approved for venues, leaves the choice with the group and never invents a standard. Put the research on Bob's list with a trigger (for example, 'a group asks what bar to use'). Separately, BOB corrects the leftover 'strictest wins' in Publication's term table, which DEC-72 removed. (Recommendation, not canon.)
howToAnswer: As recommended.
As recommended, and start the audience research now with newspapers and small-claims court.
A only: no audience presets, ever. The group decides.
What would the first profile's entry for a newspaper look like?
brief.ifLeftOpen: The bar keeps working as a bare letter the owner picks. Design words the chooser without audience guidance, and Publication §7 stays owed.

openQuestions.question: How is an out-of-view ancestor or withheld dependent phrased so it states incompleteness and nothing else?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: DEC-36 is absolute on identity and detail; a later session must not 'fix' it toward silence.
openQuestions.context: Sometimes something a member is looking at rests on, or feeds into, material they are not allowed to see, such as a question in a project they have not joined. The product must tell them the picture is incomplete without revealing anything about the hidden material. Members meet it in the queue, on strength panels and in re-evaluation.

canonSays.says: An invisible ancestor 'is stated as an incompleteness and disclosed as nothing else': identity and detail are absolute ('no id, no title, no state, no count'); the fact that something is missing is stated; 'a later session must not... fix it toward silence.'
An ancestor the viewer may not see is not named and adds out_of_view, which makes the case set 'undetermined'.
Each hidden bundle id is replaced by null in the members and by 'an object you may not see' in the prose, with out_of_view when anything was withheld.

canonSays.source: reevaluation R3, R7, R20; connections R20
canonSays.says: A dependent the viewer may not see is 'withheld whole, with no count'; backlinks list only visible citers, 'no count of what was withheld'.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The requirements do not agree with each other on how to follow DEC-36. The queue and strength state the incompleteness; the re-evaluation and backlink reads withhold silently with no marker, which is exactly the 'silence' DEC-36 forbids. Strength R6 places one 'object you may not see' per hidden member, which lets a reader count them, and DEC-36 forbids counts.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The old interface shows a sentence such as 'Part of what this is filed under is not visible to this credential, so the list... is incomplete rather than settled' in the queue, and a similar line on strength panels, with no count.
related: Q6 the one treatment of UNDETERMINED versus withheld

options.option: One fixed sentence, one visual marker, used everywhere something is hidden: 'Something this rests on is outside what you can see; this list is incomplete.'
options.tradeoffs: Consistent and teachable; requires the re-evaluation and backlink reads to add a marker and strength R6 to drop its per-item placeholders (requirement changes).

options.option: Keep each surface's wording but standardise the marker and forbid counts, placeholders and positions.
options.tradeoffs: Smaller change; wording drift continues.

options.option: Add who to ask ('a member of the project that holds it can see it') to the sentence.
options.tradeoffs: More helpful; may itself reveal that a project exists, which DEC-36 may forbid.

openQuestions.recommendation: Adopt the single sentence and marker, and have BOB record a ruling that re-evaluation, backlinks and strength R6 conform (state the incompleteness, no counts). Do not add the 'who to ask' hint.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob, for the scope: whether DEC-36's rule (a missing item is stated as missing, never named or counted) also governs hidden dependents and backlinks, which today are withheld silently. Design then settles the one sentence and marker within DEC-86. Strength's count leak was corrected in T12 (N303, K360).

brief.settledBy: Partly. DEC-86: 'Withheld' has 'its own visibly distinct treatment and one fixed sentence pattern'. Strength R6 (K360, built T12) now withholds hidden members 'whole ... no placeholder and no count, and out_of_view: true stating only that something was withheld', which closes the count leak. DEC-85 and K523: hidden conflicting projects may be 'noticed only on the member's own side, never named'. Still open: reevaluation R3, R7, R20 and connections R20 still withhold hidden dependents and backlinks silently ('no count of what was withheld', and no marker). N320 finds the countable-placeholder pattern in conformance, consequences, escalation and filings, 'worded once he rules'.
brief.title: Saying 'there is more you cannot see' about work that depends on this
brief.decision: Does DEC-36's rule apply downstream as well as upstream? The rule: a hidden item is never named or counted, but the fact that something is missing is stated. Downstream means other work that rests on, or cites, what the member is looking at. Today that work is left out without a word.
brief.whyYours: DEC-36 is Bob's doctrine on sight, and he said a later session 'must not ... fix it toward silence'. Whether it reaches downstream decides what members are told about projects they cannot see. The sentence and the mark are Design's (DEC-86).
context: A group's copy of CivicOS holds many projects, and each member sees only some of them. DEC-36 settled the upstream direction: if something your work rests on is out of your view, the screen says the picture is incomplete, with no id, title, state or count.

The downstream direction works differently today. When a member changes something, for example marking a capture as superseded, the re-evaluation panel lists what must be looked at again, but only what the member can see, with no hint that anything else exists. 'Cited by' lists behave the same way. Example: Maya marks a budget PDF as superseded. The panel says '2 questions rest on this'. Three more rest on it in a confidential project. She is not told, and she may judge the change minor. (That project's own members still get their notices.)
Bob has already accepted a similar disclosure. Under DEC-85, a project is told 'something this project rests on is in conflict with a record you cannot see', without naming the other project.
alreadySettled: DEC-36: no id, title, state or count of what is hidden; the incompleteness is stated; never 'fixed toward silence' (Interaction Constructs).
DEC-86: 'Withheld' has its own treatment and fixed sentence, distinct from Undetermined, Unrated, Nobody looked and Refused.
Strength R6 (K360): hidden members are withheld whole and only out_of_view is stated. Queue R7: a hidden ancestor makes the item's home set 'undetermined'.
DEC-85 and K523: a hidden conflicting project is noticed only on the member's own side, never named.

options.label: A
options.name: State it wherever something was withheld
options.whatTheMemberSees: '2 questions you can see rest on this. Others you cannot see may also rest on it, so this list is incomplete.' It is shown only when something was withheld, in the Withheld style, with no count.
options.gains: One rule everywhere, consistent with DEC-36 and DEC-85.
options.costs: It reveals one bit: that some hidden work uses this item. Reevaluation, connections and N320's four modules need their wording changed.

options.label: B
options.name: The same caveat on every downstream list
options.whatTheMemberSees: Every dependents and 'cited by' list carries 'Only what you can see is listed', whether or not anything is hidden.
options.gains: Reveals nothing, not even that hidden work exists.
options.costs: Less informative, and members learn to ignore a line that is always there. It is arguably not the 'stated incompleteness' DEC-36 asks for.

options.label: C
options.name: Keep downstream lists silent
options.whatTheMemberSees: Lists show only visible items, with no remark.
options.gains: No change needed.
options.costs: Keeps downstream the silence DEC-36 forbids upstream, and members misjudge how far a change reaches.

brief.recommendation: A. It applies Bob's own rule consistently, and DEC-85 already accepted the one bit it reveals. If Bob thinks even the existence of hidden downstream work is too much to reveal, B is the safe fallback. Either way there are no counts, placeholders or positions, and BOB then rewords reevaluation R3, R7 and R20, connections R20 and N320's four modules to match. (Recommendation, not canon.)
howToAnswer: As recommended.
B: one standing line on every list, never conditional.
A for re-evaluation, but leave backlinks silent.
Could someone use option A to probe whether a confidential project exists?
brief.ifLeftOpen: Downstream lists stay partial without saying so, N320's wording waits, and the redesign applies 'Withheld' upstream only.

openQuestions.question: How does the product present the difference between the working side and the published side so a member always knows which side of the fence they are on?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: The privacy fence is architectural; working and published material must never share surface ambiguity.
openQuestions.context: CivicOS holds two kinds of material: the working record (private material the group is still judging) and the published record (cases the group has signed and released, which anyone can read and verify). This 'privacy fence' is built into the system, not just the look of the screens. Members cross between the two constantly.

canonSays.says: 'Working-corpus material and published material never share a surface ambiguity. A member always knows which side of the fence they are looking at.'
A review copy 'never leaves the instance', is mutable and marked as what it is; an outside recipient reads it through a revocable grant, and it can be exported with an in-band notice on every page.

canonSays.source: DEC-19; Interaction Constructs rung ladder; K356
canonSays.says: Publishing is the only irreversible act; K356 names the sequence release to publish the 'path to publication'.
Working material 'answers an outsider exactly as something that does not exist'.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The principle is stated but no design says how the two sides look. The review copy blurs the fence: it is working material, yet a person without an account can read it and a member can export it, while the old semantics table defines the working record as 'never served to anyone without a credential'. The canon does not say whether there are two spaces or three (working, review copy, published), or how the path to publication is shown as crossing.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The old interface uses two separate spaces: the member app has a persistent footer 'Working record · not public', and the published space has its own masthead, with the semantics table defining 'working record' and 'published record'.

options.option: Two spaces with distinct frames (colour, masthead, wording), and the review copy shown in the working frame with a 'review copy, not published' band.
options.tradeoffs: Simple and matches the architecture; the recipient's view of a review copy needs its own careful marking.

options.option: Three named spaces: working, shared for review, published.
options.tradeoffs: Most accurate to what a member can do; adds a concept to learn.

options.option: Two spaces plus a fence marker on every object showing which side it is on and where it sits on the path to publication.
options.tradeoffs: Strong signal at object level; busier screens.

openQuestions.recommendation: Use two spaces with distinct frames plus a per-object path-to-publication marker, and treat the review copy as a working-side object with its own band; correct the semantics table's 'never served without a credential' wording.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Design, within Bob's stated principle; Bob only if the designer proposes a third space, since that changes how members are taught the fence.

brief.settledBy: Partly. The crossing is designed: the ceremony (DEC-80) with 'the path to publication' (K356). What crosses discloses each document's grade (DEC-81), any unresolved record contradiction (DEC-76 (4)), and a conflict with a hidden record (DEC-85). Another group's work carries an origin mark (DEC-92). The Action layer adds a second outward path: filings and messages leave only by a member's own hand, stamped in-band (filings R22-R23; K597 (5), 'nothing non-public leaving by a system path'). How the two sides look remains open.
brief.title: Always knowing which side of the privacy fence you are on
brief.decision: Should members learn two spaces (working and published), with review copies and outgoing drafts shown as clearly marked working-side items? Or three (working, shared for review, published)? Colours, mastheads and markers are Design's.
brief.whyYours: Mostly Design's, honestly. Bob's principle is set: 'a member always knows which side of the fence they are looking at.' Bob's only piece is how many spaces members are taught, because that is how the fence is taught.
context: The working record is the group's private material. The published record is what the group has signed and released for anyone to read and verify. The only way across is the publication ceremony (DEC-80), and publishing cannot be undone.

Some things sit in between. A review copy is a draft case a named outsider reads through a revocable link: it never leaves the group's copy and is marked 'not a publication'. Since the Action design there are also filings and messages that a member prepares, stamps and sends by their own hand. Example: Luis grants a city-hall reporter a review link to a draft case, and the reporter reads it in a browser without an account. It is not published, but it is no longer purely internal either.
The old interface used two spaces: a member app with the footer 'Working record · not public', and a public site with its own masthead.
alreadySettled: 'Working-corpus material and published material never share a surface ambiguity' (UI-KICKOFF, constraints that are law).
Working material 'answers an outsider exactly as something that does not exist' (publication R29).
A review copy never leaves the instance, can be revoked, is marked as what it is, and carries an in-band notice when exported (Publication §6A).
Publishing is the only irreversible act, crossed through the five-step ceremony (DEC-19, DEC-80), and the sequence is called the 'path to publication' (K356).
Filings, packets and messages carry an in-band stamp and are sent by the member, never by the system (filings R22-R23, K597 (5), DEC-31).

options.label: A
options.name: Two spaces; in-between things carry a band
options.whatTheMemberSees: The member app in its working frame. A review copy or outgoing draft appears inside it with a band such as 'Review copy: shared with 1 person, not published'. The public site has its own masthead.
options.gains: Simple, and it matches the architecture.
options.costs: The recipient's view of a review copy needs its own careful marking.

options.label: B
options.name: Three named spaces
options.whatTheMemberSees: A third frame, 'Shared for review', with its own colour, holding review copies.
options.gains: Accurate to what a member can do.
options.costs: One more concept to learn, and outgoing action messages do not fit it neatly, since they leave the system.

options.label: C
options.name: Two spaces, plus a path marker on every object
options.whatTheMemberSees: As A, plus a small step marker on each document or case: working → shared for review → published.
options.gains: A strong signal on each object.
options.costs: Busier screens.

brief.recommendation: A with C's marker: two spaces with distinct frames, a path-to-publication marker on each object, and review copies and outgoing drafts shown as working-side items with their own band. Bob need only confirm 'two spaces', and the rest goes to Design. BOB corrects the old semantics table's 'never served to anyone without a credential', which the review copy contradicts. (Recommendation, not canon.)
howToAnswer: As recommended.
Three spaces.
Two spaces; leave the markers to Design.
brief.ifLeftOpen: Design works to Bob's principle, with the old interface's two spaces as the default. Nothing waits.

openQuestions.question: How are declared flows (progressions) and their deltas drawn so the analytic product (declared vs observed flow) is visible, and our own missed deadlines are never shown as findings about the world?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: The delta is the product; conflating plans with progressions converts a management fact into evidence.
openQuestions.whereTheCanonStops: NOTIFICATIONS.md (D-128); Case Making action plan section 3
openQuestions.context: A 'progression' is a declared model of how a public body is supposed to act, for example minutes follow a meeting, an award follows a solicitation. Members thread real documents into it, and the system shows where reality departed: a missing earlier step, a late later step, or too many documents at one stage. Separately, an 'action plan' is the group's own steps and deadlines.

canonSays.says: 'The analytic product is the DELTA. Declared flow versus observed flow'; a civic obligation (the body's duty) is not a member task, and 'naming them one thing would have modelled our inbox and called it the institution.'
Plans and progressions 'MUST NOT SHARE AN OBJECT': otherwise 'our own missed deadline would surface as a finding about the record — converting a management fact into evidence.'
Progression divergences reach the queue as FINDING items (shown to members as 'Noticed'); the queue's OBLIGATION class holds member tasks and bias debt.

openQuestions.whyOpen: The data exists but no design draws it. D-128's 'flow model' home is still open, and there is no module for the action plan (S11), so nothing yet keeps the two visibly apart. The queue's OBLIGATION class holds member tasks while Bob's ruling says OBLIGATION means the body's own duty, so the labels invite the conflation the canon warns against.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The old interface has a Progressions screen that lists declared stages with threaded documents and text findings; it draws no timeline or declared-versus-observed chart and has no action-plan surface.

options.option: A swim-lane timeline per instance: declared stages as a ghost track, observed documents placed on it, gaps and late steps marked in the record's words.
options.tradeoffs: Makes the delta the picture; needs care with undetermined dates and grades.

options.option: A table of instances by stage with divergence counts, drilling into a single instance's timeline.
options.tradeoffs: Scales to many instances; the story is less immediate.

options.option: Keep our own plans on a separate surface with a different visual language (a checklist or task board, never the timeline style).
options.tradeoffs: Guards the doctrine structurally; needs the S11 design to exist.

openQuestions.recommendation: Use the timeline with a summary table above it for the world, and a visibly different surface for our own plans. Ask Bob whether to relabel the queue's member-task class so it no longer carries the word 'obligation'.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Design for the drawing; Bob for any relabelling of the OBLIGATION class, since it is his ruled vocabulary.

rulings: K611 (the overdue clock is a CONDITION)
ruled.title: Our own missed deadlines are never findings
ruled.decided: For plans: a plan's checkpoints are the group's own intentions. A missed or not-met checkpoint is never a finding, a condition of the record or a fact about the government; its reminder is an obligation of the group's own, shown as ours. The counterparty's deadline is a condition on the action, raised once when overdue. How declared flows and their deltas are drawn remains Design's.
ruled.stillOpen: the word members see for the queue's to-do class

brief.settledBy: Answered for plans. UX-ANSWERS.md (approved by Bob 2026-09-30, K608 (4)): 'OQ-25 ... answered for plans (the OBLIGATION relabelling stays Bob's)': 'a missed or not_met checkpoint is never a finding, a condition of the record or a fact about the government (action-plans R23)'. queue-producers R16: a checkpoint item 'is never a FINDING'. K611 and K624 (4): an action's overdue clock (the other side's deadline) is a CONDITION. How declared flows and their gaps are drawn is Design's. What is left for Bob is the relabelling, explained here.
brief.title: What to call the queue's to-do items (the OBLIGATION relabelling)
brief.decision: Should the queue's OBLIGATION class, meaning things a named member must do, be shown to members under another name such as 'To do'? Then 'obligation' in the product would mean only a public body's duty, as Bob ruled on 2026-08-01.
brief.whyYours: It is Bob's own ruled vocabulary, and UX-ANSWERS, which he approved, leaves it to him by name. How the chip looks is Design's. Renaming the internal code is a technical call for BOB.
context: The queue is each member's list of 'things that want me', grouped by the case they belong to. Its items fall into three classes. OBLIGATION: something a named person must do. FINDING: something the record noticed that nobody has judged yet, shown to members as 'Noticed' since K356. CONDITION: a signal, mostly about the system's own machinery.

On 2026-08-01 Bob said obligations are 'the flows (edges) that go on in a living civic system': a public body's duties, such as posting minutes within 10 days of a meeting. The canon added that calling member tasks by the same name 'would have modelled our inbox and called it the institution.' Yet the queue class kept the name, and it now holds more and more of the group's own work: plan checkpoints, reminders a member asked for, proposed escalation steps, contradictions a project must resolve, bias debts, self-registered signing keys.

Meanwhile 'obligation' also appears in its civic sense, on screens members and readers see. An 'obligation against act' finding (the law required X, the city did Y) is published in the audit form Criteria, Condition, Cause, Effect (DEC-76, DEC-84). Example: Rosa's queue shows 'OBLIGATION · Checkpoint: the city shows earnest commitment' directly above 'Noticed · Obligation against act: minutes not posted within 10 days'. The first is her group's own intention; the second is the city's legal duty. It is the same word for opposite owners.
alreadySettled: A missed plan checkpoint is the group's own, never a finding, a condition of the record or a fact about the government (action-plans R23; queue-producers R16; UX-ANSWERS, approved K608 (4)).
The other side missing its deadline is a CONDITION on the action, which notifies once (K611; K624 (4); DEC-94 (4)).
The FINDING class is shown as 'Noticed', its code unchanged (K356).
Queue items must show 'whose obligation it is: the group's own (checkpoint) or the counterparty's (deadline)' (Action design PATH.md §3).

options.label: A
options.name: 'To do' as the members' label; code unchanged
options.whatTheMemberSees: 'To do · Checkpoint: the city shows earnest commitment'. The word 'obligation' appears only for a body's duty.
options.gains: Mirrors K356, costs only a label, and ends the clash.
options.costs: Internal documents keep OBLIGATION, so builders and members use different words, as they already do for FINDING.

options.label: B
options.name: Rename the class everywhere
options.whatTheMemberSees: The same as A. In addition, canon, requirements and code call it TASK or DUTY.
options.gains: One word at every layer.
options.costs: A large mechanical rename for BOB to schedule, with no difference members can see.

options.label: C
options.name: Keep 'obligation' and name the owner
options.whatTheMemberSees: 'Our obligation · Checkpoint ...' beside 'The city's obligation · minutes ...'.
options.gains: Keeps Bob's word and makes ownership explicit, as the Action design already phrases it.
options.costs: The word still means two things, and everything depends on the qualifier being read.

brief.recommendation: A. It completes what K356 started (a plain member word over an unchanged code) and gives 'obligation' back to the institution. Whether the code is ever renamed (B) is technical and can go to BOB. The Action design's 'an obligation of the group's own' would then read 'the group's own to-do'. (Recommendation, not canon.)
howToAnswer: As recommended.
As recommended, but call it 'For you' rather than 'To do'.
C: keep 'obligation' and name whose it is.
B: rename it everywhere.
brief.ifLeftOpen: The redesigned queue shows 'obligation' for member tasks, the clash with civic obligations stays, and the three labels in Q28 wait on this one.
sources: NOTIFICATIONS.md 'OBLIGATION is the civic system's own flows' and 'Presented and treated differently'
ux-substrate-v2.json glossary 'Queue' (drafts 'to-dos, things noticed, and signals')

openQuestions.question: What does the knocker, and the member at the doorbell, see when the rate bound is hit (no translation yet, D-508)?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: A refusal must teach; a 429 is a claim that needs a count behind it.
openQuestions.context: The 'doorbell' lets anyone, with no account, hand a group a document (a 'knock'). To stop one sender or a flood filling the group's inbox, the instance limits knocks: 12 per sender and 300 in total in any 10 minutes. The person knocking (the knocker) meets the limit when they are refused; members meet the doorbell when they review the inbox.

canonSays.says: 'A 429 tells a member of the public they knocked too often, which is a claim that needs a count behind it'; the bound is published with its method ('at most 12 knocks from one source in any 10 minutes, estimated by a sliding window').
RATE_IP and RATE_GLOBAL 'have no member-facing translation yet'.

The refusal carries the catalogue row's translation plus the stated bound; nothing is stored or counted. A code without a translation 'never reaches a knocker as a bare code: the doorbell fails as an internal error instead.'

openQuestions.whyOpen: The canon is behind the code: the plane's catalogue now has plain-language translations for both refusals, yet the doctrine still says none exist, so what the knocker sees has been drafted by a builder and never reviewed. Nothing on the member side exists: refusals are not stored, so members cannot learn their doorbell is saturated, although the RATE_GLOBAL wording tells the knocker 'the group's members can be told'. There is also no public knock page, only the programme call.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: Nothing for the knocker (no public knock form); members see the inbox list on the setup page with 'Mark as taken up' and 'Set aside', and nothing about refused knocks.
related: Q2 how a knock becomes part of the record

options.option: Adopt the plane's existing translations with the stated bound and a 'try again after' hint for the knocker; members see nothing.
options.tradeoffs: Cheap and consistent with 'nothing is counted'; the RATE_GLOBAL wording's promise to members becomes false and should be removed.

options.option: Record a count-only saturation signal (no fingerprints, no content) and show members a condition 'the doorbell turned people away N times today'.
options.tradeoffs: Members learn of floods or attacks; needs a new requirement and a privacy check that the count reveals nothing.

openQuestions.recommendation: Review and adopt the existing translations now, with the public page showing the bound, and ask Bob whether members should see a count-only saturation signal; until he rules, drop the 'members can be told' sentence.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Design for the knocker's wording and page; Bob for whether refused knocks are recorded at all, which changes what the record holds.

brief.settledBy: Partly changed, not settled. DEC-78 (a knock's source is an unnamed knocker; an optional knocker secret proves continuity). K509 (3): doorbell material is graded 'received'. K530 and sources R11: a source giving or withdrawing consent with their secret is 'rate-bound as a knock is, in the same windows as knocks'. Still as built: capture R47-R48 say 'Nothing is stored and nothing is counted', and the Intake Doctrine status line still says RATE_IP and RATE_GLOBAL 'have no member-facing translation yet (D-508)', although the catalogue holds unreviewed translations (C-85.1, C-85.2).
brief.title: When the doorbell is full: what the sender and the group are told
brief.decision: Should the group's members learn that their doorbell has been turning people away, as a bare count with nothing about who? Or should refused knocks stay entirely unrecorded, in which case the refusal text stops promising that 'the group's members can be told'?
brief.whyYours: Whether refused knocks are recorded at all changes what the record holds about members of the public, which is intake doctrine (Intake Doctrine §2a). The sender's wording and the public page are Design's.
context: The doorbell lets anyone, with no account, hand a group a document (a 'knock'), optionally with a note and a secret that proves several knocks came from the same person. The limit is 12 knocks per sender and 300 in total in any 10 minutes. Over the limit the sender is refused, and nothing is stored or counted.

Refusal texts exist, drafted by a builder and never reviewed. The one for a full instance ends: 'If it keeps happening, the group's members can be told the doorbell is saturated.' Nothing records that it happened, so members cannot be told.

Since DEC-78, a source's consent by secret counts against the same limits. Example: during a controversy a hostile party floods a group's doorbell. A whistleblower trying to send a second document, or to consent to publishing their job title, is turned away for hours. The members see a quiet inbox and assume nothing is coming.
alreadySettled: A refusal carries its translation and the stated bound; nothing is stored or counted; a code without a translation never reaches a sender bare (capture R47-R48, R52).
A knock's source is an unnamed knocker; the contact stays in the inbox (DEC-78). Doorbell material is graded 'received' (K509 (3)).
Consent by secret counts in the same windows as knocks (sources R11, K530).
A 'noticed' condition shows as status where the thing lives, not as a queue item (NOTIFICATIONS.md).

options.label: A
options.name: Record nothing; fix the text
options.whatTheMemberSees: The sender sees the refusal, the bound and 'try again in about N minutes'. Members see nothing.
options.gains: Nothing about the public is stored.
options.costs: The group never learns of floods, and the 'members can be told' sentence must go.

options.label: B
options.name: A count-only status on the doorbell
options.whatTheMemberSees: The sender sees the same as A. On the doorbell page members see 'Turned away 214 knocks today (limit reached 3 times; last at 14:05)', with no addresses, fingerprints or content.
options.gains: The group learns of floods or attacks and can publicise another way in.
options.costs: 'Nothing is counted' becomes 'only a daily total', which needs a requirement change and a check that the total reveals nothing.

options.label: C
options.name: B, plus one to-do when it lasts
options.whatTheMemberSees: As B, and when the instance limit holds for (say) an hour, administrators get one queue item: 'The doorbell has been full for an hour.'
options.gains: Reaches administrators who do not open the doorbell page.
options.costs: Closer to nagging, even as a single item, and more to design.

brief.recommendation: B. The doctrine itself says a refusal is 'a claim that needs a count behind it', and an instance-wide total helps the group without saying anything about any sender. Keep it as status on the doorbell page, not a queue item, in line with Bob's no-nagging rulings. Design then reviews the two refusal texts and the public page. (Recommendation, not canon.)
howToAnswer: As recommended.
A: record nothing, and strike the promise.
C: I want administrators told when it lasts.
Could the daily total itself tell an attacker anything?
brief.ifLeftOpen: Refusals keep working as built. The full-instance text keeps a promise nothing fulfils (BOB can strike that sentence meanwhile), and members stay unaware of floods.

openQuestions.question: How is the founder / root-of-trust responsibility explained, given custody is unmodelled (DEC-2 deferred)?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Losing or leaking it has costs the group should understand at claim time.
openQuestions.context: When a group installs CivicOS, the installer produces a one-time password (technically the ADMIN_TOKEN) and the founder uses it to 'claim' the copy and set their own password. Whoever controls the group's hosting account can reset that token and take the instance back, which makes the hosting account the real 'root of trust'.

canonSays.says: What a root of trust should be is deferred until 'a BIO instance running with MULTIPLE MEMBERS' shows what a real group can hold; the alternative is to 'document the limit honestly, which is what is happening by default.'
'Whoever can set ADMIN_TOKEN can take the group over... The holders of ADMIN_TOKEN are the root of trust.'
Hosting access should be separated from administrator status; 'no interface may imply otherwise' than that governance cannot decide who runs the machine.
The token has no custody model, no audit trail and no rotation short of returning the instance to unclaimed; until designed, root of trust means 'whoever controls the hosting account'.

openQuestions.whyOpen: Bob has deferred the policy, so the design can only explain the current arrangement, but no text decides how much to say or when. The current claim page frames the hosting sign-in only as a reassuring way back in ('you are not locked out'), while §4.6 says the same power lets anyone holding it take the group over, and §4.8 forbids an interface that implies governance controls the machine. What the founder must be told, and whether to acknowledge it, is unwritten.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The setup page tells the founder that losing the password is recoverable by replacing ADMIN_TOKEN in Cloudflare ('Your Cloudflare sign-in is the way back in'), and says nothing about takeover risk or who should hold hosting access.
related: UC-030 verified export gated on the token

options.option: A short plain explainer at claim: who holds the hosting account holds the group; keep it separate from administrators; what losing or leaking it costs.
options.tradeoffs: Honest and cheap; adds reading at a moment founders want to get started.

options.option: A standing 'custody' card in administrator settings that restates the risk and shows when the token last changed (the plane can detect a change).
options.tradeoffs: Keeps the fact visible beyond day one; the detected change is only partial evidence.

openQuestions.recommendation: Adopt the explainer at claim plus the standing custody card, and correct the claim page's one-sided reassurance; leave any acknowledgement act until DEC-2's trigger fires.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Bob for what the group is told about a policy he deferred (a doctrine-adjacent disclosure); Design for placement and wording once he agrees.

brief.settledBy: Not settled. DEC-2 (custody) stays deferred. DEC-80 (4) only makes the founder's delivery of signatures a fallback. Already built around it: membership R11 (when a second administrator is added, 'the group is asked to record who holds hosting access, and the record keeps the answer'), R7 (removing the founder is refused ROOT_OF_TRUST, 'naming the hosting account as the remedy') and R8.
brief.title: What the founder is told about who really controls the group's copy
brief.decision: What is the person who installs and claims CivicOS told about the 'root of trust', meaning that whoever controls the group's hosting account can take the whole copy over? Is it said once at claim, kept visible in administrator settings, or both?
brief.whyYours: Bob deferred the custody policy itself (DEC-2). Deciding how a group is told about a risk he left unmodelled is a disclosure close to doctrine. Placement and wording are Design's.
context: The founder is the person who installs the group's copy and claims it with a one-time password (the ADMIN_TOKEN) held in the group's Cloudflare hosting account. Anyone who can change that setting can reset it and take the copy back. Membership v2 §4.6: 'Whoever can set ADMIN_TOKEN can take the group over.' Administrator votes cannot overrule whoever runs the hosting account, and 'no interface may imply otherwise' (§4.8).

Today's claim page treats the hosting sign-in only as reassurance: 'Your Cloudflare sign-in is the way back in.' Example: a founder uses her personal Cloudflare account and later leaves the group after a dispute. The remaining administrators vote to remove her, and the product refuses (ROOT_OF_TRUST), because she is the root of trust. She can still reset the password and read everything.

Custody has no model: there is no audit trail for the token, and no way to rotate it short of returning the copy to unclaimed. Bob deferred designing custody until a real multi-member group shows what it can manage.
alreadySettled: DEC-2 is deferred; meanwhile the limit is documented honestly.

'The holders of ADMIN_TOKEN are the root of trust' (Membership v2 §4.6). Hosting access is separate from administrator status (§4.8). Until custody is designed, the root of trust is 'whoever controls the hosting account' (§9).

Removing the founder is refused, naming the hosting account (membership R7). An ejection's answer says rotating the root and reviewing hosting access is the other half (R8). The group records who holds hosting access when the second administrator is added (R11).
Once owners sign in the browser, founder delivery of signatures is only a fallback (DEC-80 (4)).

options.label: A
options.name: One plain explainer at claim
options.whatTheMemberSees: Before setting a password: 'Whoever controls this Cloudflare account controls this copy: they can reset your password and read everything. Keep that account with people the group trusts, and keep it separate from who administers the group. If it is lost or leaked, ...'
options.gains: Honest, at the moment it matters.
options.costs: More reading just when founders want to start.

options.label: B
options.name: A standing custody card
options.whatTheMemberSees: In administrator settings: who the group recorded as holding hosting access (R11), the same explanation, and 'the one-time password last changed on ...' where the system can detect a change.
options.gains: Visible to every administrator beyond day one.
options.costs: A detected change is only partial evidence.

options.label: C
options.name: A and B, plus a recorded acknowledgement
options.whatTheMemberSees: The founder and the second administrator each record 'I have read this' as an attributed act.
options.gains: A record that the group was told.
options.costs: Gets ahead of DEC-2's deferred custody design and adds ceremony.

brief.recommendation: A and B together, correcting the claim page's one-sided reassurance. Leave any acknowledgement act until DEC-2's trigger fires. (Recommendation, not canon.)
howToAnswer: As recommended.
A only; no settings card.
C: I want an acknowledgement on record.
brief.ifLeftOpen: The redesign keeps the claim page's current wording, which tells only half the story. Nothing else waits.

openQuestions.question: How are the three queue classes presented differently while remaining one queue (findings compose into cases, obligations into a flow model, conditions into status on the thing)?
openQuestions.whyItMatters: Bob ruled they deserve different treatment; each has its own home beyond the queue.
openQuestions.context: The queue is the member's daily list of 'things that want me', grouped by the case they belong to. It holds three classes of item: obligations (work assigned to someone), findings (something the system noticed, like a missing step in a declared flow) and conditions (signals about the system's own work, such as a capture waiting). Bob ruled they are one list but deserve different treatment, and each also has a home of its own elsewhere in the product.

canonSays.says: 'The QUEUE stays ONE surface'; findings compose into a case, obligations populate a flow model of the institution, conditions accumulate into a signal history 'mostly read as status on the thing'.
Recorded (never surfaces), noticed (surfaces as status where the thing lives), actionable (earns a queue item).
The queue class FINDING is shown to members as 'Noticed', its code unchanged.

Order is obligations, findings, conditions; obligations are member tasks and bias debt; a finding 'never reads as an obligation' and leaves only by a recorded disposition; conditions can only be muted.

openQuestions.whyOpen: K356 settles the finding class's label but not the treatment of the three. It also creates a word clash: 'noticed' is already the name of the condition disposition that is shown as status and not in the queue. Two of the three homes are not designed (the flow model is D-128, still open; the signal history has no requirement), so the queue cannot yet point into them. And the obligation class holds member tasks while Bob's ruling uses 'obligation' for the body's civic duty.
openQuestions.todayInOldUI: The old interface shows one list grouped by case, each item with a raw class chip (OBLIGATION, FINDING, CONDITION) and class-specific buttons (resolve or forward, decide, mute).

options.option: Three plain labels ('To do', 'Noticed', 'Status'), each with its own icon, act row and a link to its home; the condition label avoids the word 'noticed'.
options.tradeoffs: Clear and resolves the clash; condition's 'Status' label must be agreed.

options.option: Keep one mixed list ordered as today and differentiate only by chip and acts.
options.tradeoffs: Least change; does not meet Bob's 'treated differently' ruling well.

openQuestions.recommendation: Use distinct labels, icons and act rows with a link to each class's home, and have BOB rename the condition disposition 'noticed' so K356's 'Noticed' is unambiguous.
openQuestions.whoDecides: Design for the presentation; BOB for the vocabulary fix, recorded as a ruling; Bob only if the obligation class itself is to be renamed.

brief.settledBy: Partly. The finding class is shown as 'Noticed' (K356, built T12). A record contradiction is a duty that cannot be muted, and a world one is a lead (DEC-76 (3); DEC-84 (1)-(2)). DEC-85 adds 'contradiction-duty-unseen'. Reminders are the member's own, a nearing deadline changes only the display, and overdue notifies once (DEC-94). An overdue clock is a CONDITION (K611, K624 (4)). Still open: the label for the OBLIGATION class (Q25), and a word clash: 'Noticed' (the finding class) against 'noticed' (a condition disposition in NOTIFICATIONS.md). The clash is BOB's vocabulary fix, and no ruling has made it yet.
brief.title: The queue's three kinds of item: names and treatment
brief.decision: Should the queue's three classes have three plain names for members, such as 'To do', 'Noticed' and 'Status', each with its own look, its own buttons and a link to where that kind of work lives? The rest of the presentation is Design's.
brief.whyYours: Bob ruled the principle (one queue, three classes 'presented and treated differently', each with its own home) and owns the class vocabulary. Beyond approving the three names, this can go to Design, and the 'noticed' clash is BOB's to fix. Answering Q25 answers most of this.
context: The queue is each member's list of things that want their attention, grouped by case. Its three classes are to-dos a named member must act on (OBLIGATION), things the record noticed that nobody has judged (FINDING), and signals, mostly about the system's own machinery (CONDITION). Bob ruled on 2026-08-01 that they stay in one list but are treated differently, and that each has a home beyond it: findings build cases, obligations a model of how the institution is supposed to work, and conditions a history read mostly as status on the thing itself.

K356 named findings 'Noticed'. The canon already uses 'noticed' for one kind of condition: one shown as status where the thing lives and never in the queue. So 'Noticed' inside the queue and 'noticed' outside it are two different things.

Example of the recommended treatment, in Rosa's queue under the case 'Measure U': 'To do · Checkpoint due: the city shows earnest commitment [Met / Not met]'; 'Noticed · Minutes for the 9 Sept meeting are missing [Take up / Set aside, with a reason]'; 'Status · Budget PDF capture paused by the host's limit [Mute]'. A record contradiction appears as a To do that cannot be muted; a world contradiction appears under Noticed.
alreadySettled: One queue surface, with three homes beyond it (NOTIFICATIONS.md 'Presented and treated differently').
Order: obligations, findings, conditions (queue R6). A finding never reads as an obligation (R16). Obligations are never muted, and each leaves by its own resolving act (R12, R19; K607).
FINDING is shown as 'Noticed' (K356).
Contradiction duties and leads (DEC-84 (1)-(2); DEC-85); reminders and nearing deadlines (DEC-94); the overdue clock is a CONDITION (K611).
No severity ladder of warning and error colours (NOTIFICATIONS.md, 'three, not four severities').

options.label: A
options.name: Three plain names, three treatments
options.whatTheMemberSees: As in the example: each class with its own name, icon and buttons, and a link to the item's home.
options.gains: Clear, meets Bob's 'treated differently', and ends the word clash.
options.costs: The 'Status' name needs agreeing, and two of the homes (the flow model and the signal history) do not exist yet.

options.label: B
options.name: One mixed list, distinguished only by a chip
options.whatTheMemberSees: One list with small chips and different buttons, otherwise alike.
options.gains: The least change.
options.costs: Barely meets Bob's ruling.

brief.recommendation: A, with 'To do' settled by Q25, and BOB renaming the condition disposition 'noticed' (for example to 'shown as status') so that 'Noticed' means one thing. Until the flow model and signal history exist, each item links to the thing it is about. (Recommendation, not canon.)
howToAnswer: As recommended.
As recommended, but call conditions 'Signals'.
B.
brief.ifLeftOpen: Design proceeds with 'Noticed' and the raw class names for the other two, and the clash remains.
